IDEA:  
The effectiveness of mandatory leveling math courses on subsequent academic success differs significantly across student demographic groups, and these disparities can be quantitatively identified using publicly available datasets to motivate adaptive curricular interventions.

BACKGROUND:  
Current educational policies often assume uniform benefits from one-size-fits-all leveling math courses, despite evidence suggesting underrepresented minorities and disadvantaged students may experience unequal outcomes. However, prior studies lack rigorous, disaggregated statistical analyses that control for confounders and validate outcome proxies, leaving the question of differential effectiveness unresolved.

APPROACH:  
We propose training logistic regression models on NSCRC and IPEDS datasets to predict enrollment, course performance, and graduation from student demographics and leveling math completion, using propensity score weighting to control for baseline differences. We will quantify subgroup disparities via AUC differences, setting a >5% gap threshold as evidence of non-uniform effectiveness.

EXPERIMENT:  
The minimal experiment uses NSCRC and IPEDS public data to fit propensity score–weighted logistic regressions predicting downstream math success; subgroup AUCs for underrepresented minorities versus majority groups will be compared, with a >5% AUC gap indicating significant differential impact.

NOVELTY:  
Unlike prior work that treats leveling courses as monolithic and lacks confounder adjustment, this study rigorously applies causal-inspired weighting and disaggregated predictive modeling on large public datasets with an explicit falsification threshold, providing actionable evidence for equity-driven curricular redesign.

text:
IDEA:  
The positive effects of mandatory leveling math courses on undergraduate overall academic success and graduation rates substantially diminish after controlling for non-math GPA, indicating limited generalization of math skill gains beyond quantitative domains.

BACKGROUND:  
While mandatory leveling math courses aim to improve foundational quantitative skills with the expectation of boosting broad academic outcomes, existing evidence has not rigorously tested whether math gains translate into improved performance across non-math disciplines. This ambiguity undermines policy decisions surrounding math remediation’s scope and efficacy in fostering overall student success.

APPROACH:  
We will implement propensity score matching with comprehensive covariate adjustment—including transcript-level non-math GPA, standardized test scores, and pre-college academic indicators—to isolate the causal effect of mandatory leveling math courses on overall GPA and graduation likelihood. Robust balance diagnostics and sensitivity analyses will ensure matched groups are comparable and control for unobserved confounding related to motivation and preparation.

EXPERIMENT:  
Using the National Longitudinal Survey of Freshmen (NLSF) linked with transcript data, we will match students who completed mandatory leveling math courses to those who did not, then compare overall GPA and 6-year graduation rates before and after adjusting for non-math GPA. Effects smaller than Cohen’s d = 0.1 or odds ratio between 0.9–1.1 after adjustment will falsify the hypothesis.

NOVELTY:  
Unlike prior regression discontinuity or correlational studies, this work leverages detailed transcript and pre-college data with rigorous causal inference and measurement protocols to specifically isolate and quantify the unique, domain-general impact of math remediation on academic success, addressing key methodological critiques and confounders previously unaccounted for.

text:
IDEA:  
Predicted loss-of-function variants from UK Biobank exomes frequently fail to cause ≥50% reduction in gene expression at the single-cell level, challenging their use as reliable proxies for gene essentiality.

BACKGROUND:  
Current mutational constraint analyses assume predicted LoF variants (e.g., LOFTEE-annotated) cause functional gene inactivation reflected in reduced expression. However, these annotations ignore cellular heterogeneity, allele-specific expression, and compensatory mechanisms, leaving unresolved whether predicted LoFs truly suppress gene expression within individual cells. This gap undermines confidence in variant effect interpretation and gene essentiality inference.

APPROACH:  
We will integrate participant-level genotype data from UK Biobank exomes with matched single-cell RNA-seq data from the Human Cell Atlas by restricting analysis to individuals who are carriers or non-carriers of specific predicted LoF variants and comparing gene expression distributions within well-defined, cell type–matched subsets. Carrier status will be assigned at the donor level with rigorous adjustment for cell type composition and technical covariates, thereby isolating expression differences attributable to genotype rather than cellular heterogeneity.

EXPERIMENT:  
Using publicly available UK Biobank exomes annotated by LOFTEE and donor-matched Human Cell Atlas single-cell RNA-seq datasets (e.g., PBMC or relevant tissues), we will test whether ≥60% of predicted LoF variants produce ≥50% median expression reduction of the affected gene in carrier versus non-carrier cells of the same type. Failure to meet this threshold falsifies the baseline mutational constraint assumption.

NOVELTY:  
This is the first large-scale, single-cell resolution test of predicted LoF variant functional impact leveraging donor-matched genotype and transcriptome data, explicitly controlling for cell type and population heterogeneity—unlike prior bulk or population-level analyses, it provides a precise cellular phenotype validation framework for variant annotation models.

text:
IDEA: The positive impact of mandatory leveling math course completion on college degree attainment differs significantly across student demographic and socioeconomic groups, such that math improvements do not uniformly predict graduation outcomes.

BACKGROUND: While improving math proficiency through mandatory leveling courses is generally assumed to promote academic progression and degree completion, it remains unclear whether these benefits are equitable across diverse student populations. Existing research often overlooks potential heterogeneity in course effects related to demographic and socioeconomic factors, risking misinformed policies that assume uniform effectiveness.

APPROACH: Using logistic regression models on the public HSLS:09 dataset, we will predict degree completion from math leveling course completion, key demographic and socioeconomic covariates, and critically, their interaction terms to identify differential effects. The primary test is whether adding interaction terms increases explained variance (ΔR²) by at least 0.10, indicating meaningful heterogeneity.

EXPERIMENT: We will operationalize course completion as passing the mandatory leveling math course, a clearly defined binary variable in HSLS:09, and control for prior academic performance and available support variables to minimize confounding. Interaction effects will be tested with logistic regression, with ΔR² ≥ 0.10 as the numeric falsification threshold for significant heterogeneity.

NOVELTY: This work uniquely challenges the prevailing uniform-effect assumption by explicitly quantifying interaction effects across multiple demographic and socioeconomic groups using a rigorous, preregistered threshold for heterogeneity. It directly addresses measurement clarity and confounding concerns by using standardized completion criteria and controlling for academic supports, which prior studies have not systematically done.

IDEA:  
Mandatory leveling math courses do not significantly improve long-term STEM academic outcomes, as measured by advanced course completion, GPA, and graduation rates, challenging the assumption that short-term remediation drives sustained success.

BACKGROUND:  
Current STEM education policies often mandate leveling math courses based on the belief that early remediation leads to better long-term retention and application of mathematical skills. However, existing longitudinal datasets rarely capture explicit leveling course enrollment, and prior studies inadequately address confounding by unobserved factors such as motivation and institutional variation. This study directly tests the durability and causal impact of leveling courses on long-term STEM outcomes using robust statistical controls.

APPROACH:  
We leverage nationally representative longitudinal datasets (NLSY97, ELS:2002) and employ proxy operationalization of leveling math exposure via initial math placement scores or remedial math indicators. Using propensity score matching combined with sensitivity analyses for unmeasured confounding, we estimate effect sizes on STEM progression metrics relative to a baseline of standard course progression without leveling. We set a falsification threshold of a <5% difference in STEM outcomes with p>0.05 to reject meaningful long-term benefit claims.

EXPERIMENT:  
Analyze NLSY97 and ELS:2002 data subsets where remedial math placement is inferable, controlling for socioeconomic and prior achievement covariates, and measure STEM course completion rates, advanced STEM GPA, and graduation likelihood. Statistical estimation and inference will be completed within one week on a single GPU-enabled platform.

NOVELTY:  
This study explicitly addresses measurement ambiguity by proxying leveling exposure and rigorously tackles unobserved confounding through sensitivity checks, differentiating it from prior regression discontinuity or correlational studies that lack longitudinal breadth and causal robustness. It provides the first efficient, replicable framework to quantify and falsify the long-term impact of mandatory leveling math courses using publicly available data.

topic: Quantum error correction in NISQ devices
text:
IDEA:  
Optimization improvements in quantum circuit compilation for NISQ devices diminish rapidly beyond ~20 qubits, failing to scale effectively and yielding less than 5% relative gains compared to baseline compilation methods.

BACKGROUND:  
Current understanding assumes that advanced compilation optimizations maintain or increase their effectiveness as NISQ devices scale up, mitigating connectivity and noise challenges. However, the exponential growth in compilation complexity and heterogeneous noise profiles on larger devices may fundamentally limit these gains, a question untested rigorously on devices exceeding 20 qubits.

APPROACH:  
We will systematically compare the Qiskit transpiler’s default (level 1) and advanced (level 3 with SABRE routing) optimization strategies applied to a fixed set of publicly available circuits from QASMBench, targeting IBM Quantum devices with 5 to 27 qubits. Performance will be measured via hardware-executed randomized benchmarking to directly quantify error rates post-compilation, controlling for device calibration variability by repeated trials and temporal noise tracking.

EXPERIMENT:  
Compile and run identical benchmark circuits on IBM devices of varying sizes using both baseline and optimized compilation passes; measure the percentage reduction in circuit depth and empirically obtained error rates using interleaved randomized benchmarking. A relative improvement below 5% on devices larger than 20 qubits will falsify the scalability assumption.

NOVELTY:  
Unlike prior studies relying on compiler-reported error estimates or simulated noise, this work employs direct hardware benchmarking across multiple device sizes with rigorous statistical controls, isolating compilation effects from device noise variability and providing the first empirical scaling analysis of compilation optimization efficacy in mid-scale NISQ hardware.

topic: Quantum error correction in NISQ devices
text:
IDEA:  
Minimal quantum error correction codes applied to variational quantum algorithms on IBM Quantum Experience devices yield fidelity improvements exceeding 5% absolute beyond established noise-model-based theoretical bounds, demonstrating that existing noise assumptions underestimate practical QEC benefits in NISQ hardware.

BACKGROUND:  
Current theoretical bounds on variational quantum algorithm (VQA) fidelity rely on simplified noise models that inadequately capture hardware-specific error characteristics such as temporal correlations and crosstalk, limiting predicted circuit depth and fidelity improvements from minimal QEC. Experimental validation of these bounds is lacking, and it is unclear if minimal QEC can surpass these predicted limitations given realistic device noise. Addressing this gap is critical to understanding the practical utility of near-term QEC strategies in NISQ devices.

APPROACH:  
We simulate VQA performance using IBM Quantum Experience calibrated noise models with and without implementing minimal QEC codes (e.g., [[4,2,2]] code) on a fixed benchmark circuit, quantifying state fidelity via repeated sampling and bootstrapped uncertainty to ensure statistical significance. The key test is whether fidelity with QEC surpasses the baseline noise-model-based theoretical bound by an absolute margin >5%, with uncertainty intervals smaller than 1% to decisively exclude noise or sampling artifacts.

EXPERIMENT:  
Using IBM’s publicly available noise models and Qiskit Aer simulator, we run 10,000-shot simulations of a standard variational circuit on 5 qubits, measuring state fidelity against the ideal output state with and without minimal QEC encoding. Statistical significance is established by bootstrapping fidelity estimates across 100 independent runs; exceeding the noise-model-based theoretical fidelity bound by 5% absolute with >99% confidence constitutes a positive result.

NOVELTY:  
Unlike prior studies that accept theoretical noise bounds or rely on oversimplified noise assumptions, this work rigorously quantifies uncertainty and controls for noise model calibration, directly falsifying a precise numeric threshold using publicly accessible data and baseline models. This approach isolates genuine QEC benefits in realistic NISQ noise landscapes and sets a reproducible standard for future hardware validation across platforms.

topic: Quantum error correction in NISQ devices
text:
IDEA:  
Optimized compilation techniques, exemplified by Qiskit’s P1 transpiler level, exhibit diminishing returns on circuit fidelity and depth reductions beyond 20 qubits in NISQ devices, limiting their effectiveness for scalable quantum error correction.

BACKGROUND:  
Current assumptions hold that compilation optimizations will continue to improve NISQ device performance as qubit counts scale, enabling more complex error-corrected protocols. However, empirical validation of this assumption beyond 20 qubits is lacking, and hardware noise, topology constraints, and optimization complexity may impose hard scalability limits. Clarifying this limit is critical for guiding resource allocation in NISQ algorithm development and error correction strategies.

APPROACH:  
We will systematically compare circuits compiled with Qiskit’s P1 optimized and unoptimized settings on a curated set of publicly available benchmark circuits scaled from 10 to 25 qubits, controlling for hardware noise by performing repeated randomized benchmarking (standard RB) on fixed qubit subsets and calibrating against temporal noise fluctuations. Circuit fidelity improvements will be quantified via statistically robust RB decay parameters, avoiding unreliable large-scale tomography, and circuit depth reductions will be measured alongside connectivity-constrained SWAP overheads to isolate compilation efficacy. Consistent circuit families with uniform gate density and connectivity scaling will ensure representativeness.

EXPERIMENT:  
Run repeated standard randomized benchmarking experiments on IBM Q backends across 10, 15, 20, and 25 qubit subsets using benchmark circuits from the IBM Qiskit benchmark suite, comparing P1 optimized and unoptimized compiled versions. A fidelity improvement below 5% beyond 20 qubits will falsify the claim that compilation optimization scales effectively. Depth and SWAP count metrics will be measured directly from compiled circuits and normalized to device topology.

NOVELTY:  
This work provides the first rigorously controlled, multi-qubit-scale empirical evaluation of compilation optimization scalability in NISQ error correction contexts using standardized fidelity metrics and representative circuit families, explicitly addressing hardware noise variability and topology effects—factors overlooked in prior studies that predominantly focused on small-qubit or single-platform testing.

topic: Quantum error correction in NISQ devices
text:
IDEA: Integrating tailored quantum error correction protocols directly into compilation workflows yields at least a 10% reduction in logical error rates over state-of-the-art compilation-only baselines on NISQ devices.

BACKGROUND: Practical quantum error correction (QEC) implementation on NISQ hardware is hindered by noise and limited qubit resources, with most efforts focusing separately on hardware advances or compilation optimizations. Prevailing assumptions hold that sophisticated compilation alone suffices to suppress errors for small QEC codes, leaving unexplored whether embedding error correction protocols within compilation pipelines can provide meaningful fidelity gains. Clarifying this interplay is critical for near-term fault-tolerant quantum computing feasibility.

APPROACH: We simulate the [[5,1,3]] code using IBM Quantum Experience backend noise and calibration data to compare logical error rates between (1) circuits transpiled with advanced Qiskit optimizations and standard error mitigation, and (2) identically optimized circuits augmented with explicit syndrome extraction and error recovery embedded in the compilation process. Logical errors are measured post-error recovery with correction for syndrome measurement errors via calibration circuits to isolate genuine QEC effects.

EXPERIMENT: Run GPU-based density-matrix simulations using publicly available IBM noise models and calibration data, applying matched error mitigation protocols and normalizing circuit depth and gate count across paradigms to ensure fair comparison; declare the hypothesis confirmed if logical error rate improves by ≥10% in the integrated approach over the compilation-only baseline.

NOVELTY: This work uniquely combines tailored QEC protocol steps within automated compilation rather than treating them as separate layers, rigorously controls for syndrome measurement overhead and circuit complexity confounds, and benchmarks against realistic IBM noise models—advancing beyond prior studies that focus on hardware or compilation optimizations in isolation without integrated protocol-compilation evaluation.

topic: Quantum error correction in NISQ devices
text:
IDEA: Optimized quantum circuit compilation in NISQ devices introduces measurable error overheads exceeding 5% compared to unoptimized baselines when evaluated under realistic, device-calibrated noise models with controlled qubit mapping.

BACKGROUND: While optimized transpilation is widely believed to reduce error rates by minimizing gate counts and circuit depth, the interplay of additional gate decompositions, non-local qubit routing, and realistic noise often complicates this assumption. Existing work lacks systematic quantification of how these factors jointly affect error rates under faithful noise models and controlled qubit placement strategies.

APPROACH: We compare Qiskit circuits compiled at optimization level 0 (no optimization) against level 3 (high optimization) using IBM Quantum’s latest publicly available noise models and calibration data. Crucially, qubit mapping and routing heuristics are fixed and matched between both levels to isolate compilation overhead. Average circuit error rate is defined via simulated cross-entropy benchmarking (XEB) fidelity, providing a consistent, benchmark-appropriate metric.

EXPERIMENT: Run GPU-accelerated noise simulations on standard NISQ benchmark circuits (e.g., randomized benchmarks and quantum volume circuits) from IBM’s test suite, measuring XEB fidelity difference between optimization levels. A falsification threshold of 5% relative error increase in XEB fidelity under optimized compilation will validate the hypothesis.

NOVELTY: This study uniquely controls for qubit mapping to isolate the intrinsic overhead of compiler optimizations under realistic, time-correlated noise using a standardized, fidelity-based error metric, empirically challenging the community’s assumption that higher optimization unequivocally improves benchmark performance on NISQ hardware.

topic: Protein structure prediction beyond AlphaFold
text:
IDEA:  
AlphaFold-derived structural features alone are insufficient for accurate stability prediction of engineered proteins with multiple mutations or large insertions, and integrating experimentally validated biophysical features significantly improves prediction accuracy on such challenging variants.

BACKGROUND:  
While AlphaFold has revolutionized protein structure prediction, its utility for predicting stability changes in engineered proteins containing complex mutations remains unproven. Existing AlphaFold-based stability predictors often assume that predicted static structures fully capture determinants of stability, but engineered variants may induce structural perturbations or dynamic effects not reflected in AlphaFold models, limiting prediction accuracy.

APPROACH:  
We compare ThermoNet—an AlphaFold-based ΔΔG predictor—with a hybrid model that augments AlphaFold structural embeddings with experimentally validated biophysical descriptors such as solvent accessibility, secondary structure propensity, and residue-level flexibility metrics. Both models will be trained and evaluated on rigorously defined subsets of ProTherm variants containing ≥3 simultaneous mutations or insertions ≥5 residues, applying strict data curation to ensure consistent experimental conditions.

EXPERIMENT:  
Using the curated ProTherm subset, we measure Pearson correlation (r) of predicted versus experimental ΔΔG for ThermoNet alone versus the hybrid model, with r ≥ 0.6 as the falsification threshold for our hypothesis. Performance will be validated via stratified 5-fold cross-validation with consistent train-test splits to control for overfitting and experimental variance.

NOVELTY:  
Unlike prior studies that focus primarily on single-point mutations or rely exclusively on AlphaFold features, this work rigorously defines and isolates challenging engineered protein variants and quantitatively tests the sufficiency of AlphaFold-derived features versus integrative biophysical models under controlled conditions, providing the first clear demonstration of limitations and a path forward for hybrid approaches in protein stability prediction.

topic: Protein structure prediction beyond AlphaFold
text:
IDEA:  
A hybrid RNA 3D structure prediction pipeline that refines deep learning-derived initial models (E2Efold) with short, physics-based molecular dynamics simulations will achieve ≥1.0 Å RMSD improvement on RNA-Puzzles benchmark structures compared to E2Efold alone.

BACKGROUND:  
RNA 3D structure prediction lags behind protein structure prediction due to limited structural data and complex conformational dynamics. Current state-of-the-art deep learning methods like E2Efold are believed to be near their accuracy ceiling, constrained primarily by sparse training data. It remains unresolved whether integrating physics-based refinement can systematically and measurably improve RNA structural predictions beyond pure data-driven approaches.

APPROACH:  
We will generate initial RNA 3D models using the publicly available E2Efold predictor, then apply a standardized, short (up to 1 microsecond aggregate) molecular dynamics refinement protocol with a widely accepted RNA force field (e.g., AMBER OL3) under explicit solvent conditions. RMSD calculations will be performed on all heavy atoms after global superposition, ensuring consistent quantitative comparison. The RNA-Puzzles blind prediction targets will be strictly partitioned to exclude overlap with E2Efold training data, avoiding data leakage.

EXPERIMENT:  
Evaluate RMSD of refined versus baseline E2Efold models on the RNA-Puzzles benchmark set, using global alignment and all-heavy-atom RMSD, declaring success as a statistically significant mean RMSD reduction ≥1.0 Å across at least 10 diverse RNA targets. The refinement protocol will be pre-registered and applied uniformly to all targets to prevent post-hoc tuning or cherry-picking.

NOVELTY:  
This study directly tests the synergistic integration of physics-based molecular dynamics refinement with deep learning RNA structure prediction under rigorously controlled conditions and computational budgets, unlike prior works which rely solely on data-driven models or extensive, unscalable physics simulations. It uniquely addresses and rules out confounds related to RMSD calculation, data leakage, and overfitting through strict protocol design.

topic: Protein structure prediction beyond AlphaFold
text:
IDEA:  
Systematically evaluate whether explicit, rigorously engineered AlphaFold-derived structural and confidence features can predict multi-mutant protein stability changes with accuracy matching or exceeding Rosetta ddG, using strict homolog-exclusion splits to test generalization.

BACKGROUND:  
AlphaFold’s breakthrough in protein structure prediction has fueled expectations that its internal confidence metrics or structural outputs might serve as proxies for predicting protein stability changes (ΔΔG), especially in engineered variants with multiple mutations. However, prior studies show poor correlation of AlphaFold’s confidence scores with experimental stability for single mutations, and it remains unknown if these features generalize to complex multi-mutant libraries, limiting their practical use in protein engineering workflows.

APPROACH:  
Extract a defined set of residue-level features from AlphaFold predictions—specifically, per-residue pLDDT scores, predicted aligned errors (PAE), local structural environment descriptors (e.g., solvent accessibility, backbone torsions), and inter-residue distance matrices—then aggregate these into fixed-dimension vectors encoding spatial context around mutated sites. Train a regularized regression model (e.g., gradient boosting) to predict ΔΔG on multi-mutant variants, explicitly excluding homologous sequences and similar mutation patterns from test sets to prevent information leakage, and benchmark against Rosetta ddG predictions on the same variants.

EXPERIMENT:  
Use the ProTherm and MegaMut datasets, applying sequence and mutation pattern filtering to create non-overlapping train/test splits; evaluate prediction performance via Pearson correlation coefficient against experimental ΔΔG values, with a falsification threshold of correlation ≥ 0.65 to claim parity with Rosetta’s reported performance.

NOVELTY:  
This study provides the first rigorously controlled, feature-engineered assessment of AlphaFold-derived metrics for multi-mutant stability prediction under strict generalization constraints, addressing prior ambiguity in feature selection and dataset leakage while directly benchmarking against a standardized Rosetta baseline, thus clarifying AlphaFold’s practical predictive limits beyond single mutations.

topic: Protein structure prediction beyond AlphaFold
text:
IDEA:  
AlphaFold-derived features do not reliably predict stability changes for proteins with multiple simultaneous mutations, failing to capture non-additive mutational effects beyond single-point variants.

BACKGROUND:  
While AlphaFold representations correlate moderately with experimental ΔΔG for single mutations, it remains unclear whether these features encode sufficient information to predict stability changes in multiply mutated proteins where epistasis and cooperative effects dominate. Existing methods often assume additive mutation effects or rely on single-point mutation benchmarks, leaving a critical gap in understanding AlphaFold’s generalizability to complex mutational landscapes relevant for protein design.

APPROACH:  
Extract AlphaFold embeddings and pLDDT confidence scores for proteins with multiple simultaneous mutations from rigorously filtered, consistent-condition datasets (e.g., subsets of ProTherm and FireProtDB with matched assay conditions). Train gradient boosting regressors on these features to predict experimentally measured ΔΔG values, explicitly comparing performance against additive baselines constructed from single-point mutation predictors to isolate cooperative effects.

EXPERIMENT:  
Evaluate regression performance using Pearson’s correlation (r) on a held-out test set of multi-mutation variants; a threshold of r ≥ 0.5 falsifies the hypothesis. Control for additive effects by comparing against summed single-point ΔΔG predictions. Use cross-validation stratified by protein scaffold to prevent overfitting and perform independent validation on an external multi-mutant dataset to confirm generalization.

NOVELTY:  
This study uniquely tests AlphaFold feature generalization on multi-mutation stability beyond additive models while addressing dataset heterogeneity and overfitting concerns with strict filtering and independent validation. Unlike prior work focusing on single mutations or unfiltered datasets, it quantifies AlphaFold’s ability to capture epistasis and sets a clear numeric benchmark for performance.

topic: Protein structure prediction beyond AlphaFold
text:
IDEA: Fine-tuning AlphaFold’s internal embeddings by adding a dedicated stability prediction head trained end-to-end on ProTherm’s experimentally measured ΔΔG values will yield significantly more accurate protein stability change predictions for point mutations than any post hoc feature extraction from vanilla AlphaFold.

BACKGROUND: While AlphaFold has revolutionized protein structure prediction, directly predicting the impact of mutations on protein stability remains challenging and poorly addressed. Current post hoc approaches extracting features from vanilla AlphaFold predictions correlate weakly with experimental ΔΔG, and no study has rigorously tested if integrating stability objectives into AlphaFold’s training improves stability prediction without degrading structural accuracy.

APPROACH: We will fine-tune the pretrained AlphaFold model by appending a regression head that predicts ΔΔG from its learned protein embeddings during training on the ProTherm dataset, using a strict training/test split that prevents any sequence or mutation overlap. Structural prediction quality will be continuously monitored to detect and prevent catastrophic forgetting by employing a multitask loss that balances fold accuracy and stability regression.

EXPERIMENT: We will evaluate performance on a held-out ProTherm test set with no sequence or mutation context overlap, comparing Pearson correlation coefficients (PCC) of predicted vs. experimental ΔΔG between (1) vanilla AlphaFold features plus a fixed downstream regression (baseline), and (2) the fine-tuned model’s direct ΔΔG output; a PCC improvement ≥0.05 will confirm our hypothesis.

NOVELTY: Unlike prior work which only applies post hoc regression on fixed AlphaFold outputs, this approach jointly trains AlphaFold’s representations with explicit stability objectives, rigorously controls for data leakage, and monitors fold prediction fidelity during fine-tuning, providing the first clear proof-of-concept that stability prediction can be integrated into structure prediction networks for enhanced protein engineering applications.

topic: Federated learning with heterogeneous and non-IID data
text:
IDEA: Quantify how imperfect or delayed channel state information (CSI) degrades the convergence speed of federated edge learning with joint client scheduling and resource allocation under heterogeneous non-IID data, demonstrating a >10% increase in rounds to target accuracy compared to perfect CSI.

BACKGROUND: Joint client scheduling and wireless resource allocation algorithms for federated edge learning assume perfect and instantaneous CSI, which is unrealistic in practical wireless networks. The impact of CSI imperfections on convergence efficiency, especially under data heterogeneity and non-IID distributions, remains underexplored, leaving a critical gap in understanding real-world system performance degradation.

APPROACH: We simulate the established baseline method by Chen et al. for joint scheduling and resource allocation on the FEMNIST dataset with non-IID splits, incorporating realistic models of CSI imperfection such as additive Gaussian noise and fixed feedback delay. We measure convergence both in rounds and wall-clock time, analyze client selection distributions to isolate scheduling bias, and validate channel impairment models against wireless standards to ensure practical relevance.

EXPERIMENT: Run federated learning simulations on FEMNIST comparing perfect CSI versus imperfect/delayed CSI scenarios, measuring (1) rounds to reach 80% test accuracy, (2) total wall-clock training time, and (3) statistics of client selection frequency; a >10% increase in rounds under imperfect CSI constitutes hypothesis validation.

NOVELTY: Unlike prior work assuming perfect CSI, this study explicitly models and quantifies the convergence penalty caused by realistic CSI imperfections in joint scheduling, rigorously addresses confounding client selection biases, and reports both round and wall-clock convergence metrics, providing actionable insights for designing robust federated edge learning systems.

topic: Federated learning with heterogeneous and non-IID data
text:
IDEA:  
In large-scale federated learning with heterogeneous non-IID data, the communication overhead of SCAFFOLD’s control variates outweighs its convergence speedups, causing longer wall-clock training times than FedAvg beyond a medium client scale.

BACKGROUND:  
Federated learning algorithms like SCAFFOLD improve convergence on heterogeneous, non-IID data by correcting client drift using control variates, theoretically reducing variance and communication rounds. However, the practical impact of increased communication overhead and system-level constraints on overall training time at scale remains underexplored, leaving open whether SCAFFOLD’s benefits translate to faster real-world training compared to FedAvg.

APPROACH:  
We benchmark SCAFFOLD against FedAvg on the FEMNIST dataset distributed across 100 clients with controlled non-IID heterogeneity, measuring total wall-clock time, communication volume (bytes sent/received), and number of communication rounds to reach 80% test accuracy. The experiment uses a fixed hardware and network simulation environment with synchronous updates and uniform client scheduling to isolate algorithmic overhead. A falsification threshold is set: if SCAFFOLD’s wall-clock time exceeds FedAvg’s by more than 20%, the hypothesis is confirmed.

EXPERIMENT:  
Run synchronous federated training with FedAvg and SCAFFOLD on publicly available FEMNIST (100 clients, Dirichlet label skew), measuring wall-clock time with identical hardware/network emulation, communication bytes per round, and rounds to 80% accuracy.

NOVELTY:  
Unlike prior work focusing on convergence rounds or theoretical bounds, this study explicitly quantifies communication overhead and wall-clock time trade-offs under controlled system conditions, providing the first empirical scalability boundary for variance-reduction methods like SCAFFOLD in realistic federated settings.

topic: Federated learning with heterogeneous and non-IID data
text:
IDEA:  
The effectiveness of knowledge distillation from a global teacher to local clients in federated learning significantly decreases with increasing data heterogeneity, causing slower convergence and at least 2% lower final accuracy than FedAvg on highly non-IID CIFAR-10 partitions.

BACKGROUND:  
Federated learning under heterogeneous and non-IID data distributions suffers from client drift and unstable convergence. While knowledge distillation (KD) from a global teacher is often proposed to mitigate these issues by regularizing local models, the impact of extreme heterogeneity on KD’s actual efficacy remains unclear and potentially negative. This work directly tests whether KD’s global knowledge becomes less representative and thus detrimental as non-IID severity grows.

APPROACH:  
We implement a federated learning framework comparing FedAvg and KD-regularized local training, where the global teacher is the aggregated global model re-trained centrally each round to ensure up-to-date and representative knowledge. Both methods undergo rigorously matched hyperparameter tuning (learning rate, KD temperature, loss weights) at each heterogeneity level to eliminate tuning bias. Convergence speed is quantified by rounds to reach fixed accuracy thresholds, avoiding wall-clock time confounds.

EXPERIMENT:  
Partition CIFAR-10 among 20 clients using Dirichlet distributions with alpha values {1.0, 0.5, 0.1, 0.05}, focusing on alpha ≤ 0.1 (high non-IID). Measure convergence in communication rounds to reach 70% accuracy and final global accuracy after 200 rounds. The hypothesis is falsified if KD’s final accuracy exceeds FedAvg by ≥ 2% at these heterogeneity levels.

NOVELTY:  
This study uniquely provides a rigorously controlled, hyperparameter-balanced evaluation isolating the effect of data heterogeneity on KD’s efficacy in federated settings, with an up-to-date, centrally refreshed global teacher model—addressing previously confounded factors like stale teachers or tuning bias and clarifying KD’s limitations and potential failure modes under extreme non-IID conditions.

topic: Federated learning with heterogeneous and non-IID data
text:
IDEA:  
In highly dynamic mobile edge wireless environments with heterogeneous and non-IID data, simple random client scheduling combined with standard FedAvg achieves comparable or better convergence speed and model accuracy than optimized joint client scheduling and wireless resource allocation schemes relying on real-time channel knowledge.

BACKGROUND:  
Federated learning at the mobile edge must cope with device heterogeneity, non-IID data, and rapidly varying wireless channels, which complicate client selection and resource allocation. Existing approaches assume that optimized scheduling based on precise channel state information (CSI) reduces convergence delay and improves accuracy but neglect the impact of CSI acquisition overhead, estimation errors, and channel dynamics that may degrade such gains. The open problem is whether these complex scheduling strategies truly outperform naive random scheduling under realistic wireless conditions.

APPROACH:  
We compare FedAvg under random client scheduling (baseline) against a state-of-the-art joint client scheduling and wireless resource allocation algorithm that leverages instantaneous CSI, explicitly modeling realistic channel estimation delays, errors, and scheduling overheads. Convergence speed is measured by total wall-clock time including communication, computation, CSI acquisition, and scheduling latency. Model accuracy is evaluated on held-out test data. Both methods share identical local update configurations and stopping criteria defined as achieving 90% of the best final model accuracy or a maximum of 200 communication rounds.

EXPERIMENT:  
Run experiments on the FEMNIST dataset with a simulated mobile edge wireless channel model capturing rapid fading and estimation noise based on standard 3GPP channel models; measure convergence time in seconds including all overheads and final test accuracy. The falsification threshold is a minimum 10% improvement in convergence speed or accuracy in favor of the optimized scheme to claim superiority.

NOVELTY:  
This work is the first to rigorously incorporate realistic CSI acquisition overhead and channel estimation errors into the evaluation of joint scheduling/resource allocation for FL with heterogeneous, non-IID data, demonstrating that naive random scheduling with FedAvg can be a robust, low-complexity alternative in highly dynamic wireless settings where sophisticated schemes incur prohibitive overheads and myopic decisions.

topic: Federated learning with heterogeneous and non-IID data
text:
IDEA:  
Local-global knowledge distillation fails to significantly improve convergence speed over FedAvg in highly dynamic federated learning scenarios with frequent client dropouts and rapidly shifting non-IID data distributions.

BACKGROUND:  
Federated learning (FL) struggles with client drift caused by heterogeneous, non-IID data and inconsistent client participation, which slows global model convergence. While local-global knowledge distillation has been proposed to mitigate client drift by aligning local updates with a global teacher model, its efficacy has only been demonstrated in relatively stable FL settings. The impact of severe client churn and rapidly evolving local data distributions on the effectiveness of knowledge distillation remains an open problem.

APPROACH:  
We empirically evaluate local-global knowledge distillation against FedAvg under controlled, reproducible high-dynamism conditions by simulating frequent client dropout/arrival and abrupt local data distribution shifts on CIFAR-10 non-IID splits. Convergence speed will be measured by the number of communication rounds needed to reach a fixed global test accuracy of 70%, evaluated on a fixed held-out test set aggregated centrally. Hyperparameters and client sampling strategies are uniformly optimized and fixed across methods to isolate the effect of distillation.

EXPERIMENT:  
Run 5 independent trials of FedAvg and local-global knowledge distillation on CIFAR-10 using a non-IID Dirichlet split among 100 clients with 20% client dropout per communication round and randomized local class distribution changes every 10 rounds. Compare the average communication rounds to reach 70% global test accuracy. Declare the hypothesis supported if distillation fails to reduce communication rounds by at least 10% relative to FedAvg with statistical significance (p<0.05, Wilcoxon signed-rank test).

NOVELTY:  
This work rigorously tests the limits of local-global knowledge distillation under dynamically realistic FL conditions that include controlled client churn and non-stationary data shifts, exposing a critical boundary where distillation does not accelerate convergence. Prior work assumes stable participation and smooth data heterogeneity, whereas we systematically demonstrate and quantify failure modes in volatile environments, guiding future algorithm design for real-world FL.

topic: Causal discovery from observational data
text:
IDEA:  
Evaluate whether advanced nonlinear conditional independence tests in a novel causal discovery method outperform the simpler PCMCI baseline on limited-sample, high-dimensional real-world time series, testing if these CI tests degrade accuracy in such regimes.

BACKGROUND:  
Causal discovery from observational time series with high dimensionality and nonlinear dependencies is widely regarded as requiring sophisticated CI tests combined with machine learning for accurate inference. However, these methods are often validated on large or synthetic datasets with well-defined ground truth, leaving open whether they reliably improve causal network recovery under practical constraints of limited sample size (<500 time points) and noisy ecological or financial data. This gap risks overestimating their applicability in real-world scenarios.

APPROACH:  
We directly compare the novel CI-test-based causal discovery method to PCMCI on two publicly available datasets: GPDD (ecological nonlinear dynamics) and S&P 500 daily returns (financial data), truncated to identical small sample sizes to reflect realistic data scarcity. We use domain-expert consensus causal graphs and established proxy causal links from literature as stable ground-truth surrogates, and evaluate F1-scores for edge recovery, setting a 10% F1 improvement over PCMCI as the threshold for significance.

EXPERIMENT:  
Run both methods on the truncated GPDD and S&P 500 datasets with standardized hyperparameter tuning via nested cross-validation to avoid overfitting bias, then compute and compare F1-scores against proxy ground truths derived from well-curated domain knowledge and previous validated studies.

NOVELTY:  
Unlike prior work focused on large or simulated datasets with fully known causal graphs, this study rigorously tests nonlinear CI methods under realistic small-sample, noisy conditions on real-world ecological and financial data, explicitly addressing ground-truth ambiguity through curated proxies and stringent tuning protocols to isolate CI test limitations in practical applications.

topic: Causal discovery from observational data
text:
IDEA: Quantitatively evaluate how latent confounders impair TCDF’s ability to recover causal graphs from observational time series by applying it to controlled synthetic datasets with rigorously simulated latent variables and matched data distributions.

BACKGROUND: Robust causal discovery from observational time series is hindered by latent confounders that induce spurious correlations, yet TCDF claims effective causal graph recovery without interventions or latent variable modeling. The actual degradation of TCDF’s performance under well-defined confounding scenarios remains unquantified, limiting practical understanding of its reliability.

APPROACH: We generate paired synthetic datasets based on SynTReN or CauseMe simulators with identical causal structures and sampling parameters, introducing latent confounders as hidden common parents with precisely controlled influence strengths while maintaining matched sample sizes and noise characteristics. TCDF’s causal edge recovery F1-score is computed separately for confounded and unconfounded settings, using consistent evaluation protocols to isolate the effect of latent confounding.

EXPERIMENT: Run TCDF on publicly available SynTReN or CauseMe time series with no hidden variables and then with introduced latent confounders defined as unobserved nodes influencing at least two observed nodes; report causal edge F1-score with a falsification threshold of F1 < 0.5 in the confounded case versus > 0.7 in the unconfounded case to confirm performance degradation.

NOVELTY: This study rigorously operationalizes latent confounding in nonlinear time series causal discovery with reproducible, controlled synthetic data and matched experimental conditions, directly isolating latent confounders’ impact on TCDF—unlike prior work which lacks systematic quantification or confounding-specific sensitivity analyses in deep learning causal discovery frameworks.

topic: Causal discovery from observational data
text:
IDEA: Evaluate and quantify the degradation in PCMCI+ causal discovery performance caused solely by the introduction of rigorously defined latent confounders in nonlinear time series, using a reproducible masking protocol on publicly available climate and fMRI datasets with a >20% F1 score drop as a falsification threshold.

BACKGROUND: Current causal discovery methods based on conditional independence tests, such as PCMCI+, are widely assumed to be moderately robust to latent confounders, despite lacking rigorous empirical validation on real nonlinear time series with known hidden variables. This unverified robustness assumption risks misleading causal interpretations in high-impact domains like climatology and neuroscience, where unobserved confounding is prevalent.

APPROACH: We introduce latent confounders by systematically masking variables verified as confounders from prior domain knowledge, removing them entirely from the dataset rather than imputing or partially masking, to isolate hidden confounding effects without inducing distributional shifts or missingness artifacts. We then apply PCMCI+ to both original and confounder-masked datasets, measuring precision, recall, and F1 score changes across multiple randomized runs with statistical significance testing to ensure robust inference.

EXPERIMENT: Apply PCMCI+ to benchmark nonlinear time series datasets—specifically, climate teleconnection data and fMRI time series with established confounders—comparing causal graph recovery performance before and after masking latent confounders; a consistent >20% F1 score drop across datasets and repeats will falsify the robustness assumption.

NOVELTY: This study uniquely isolates the impact of latent confounders through a transparent, reproducible masking protocol on real nonlinear time series, rigorously quantifying PCMCI+’s sensitivity, and addressing confounding from masking artifacts and nonstationarities through controlled experimental design and repeated testing—thus providing the first clear empirical test of latent confounder robustness in a widely used causal discovery method.

topic: Causal discovery from observational data
text:
IDEA:  
Quantify the degradation in accuracy of causal network estimation by the PC algorithm combined with kernel-based conditional independence tests (PC+KCI) as the proportion of *explicitly simulated* latent confounders increases, demonstrating that latent confounding—not merely variable masking or sample size reduction—substantially impairs baseline nonlinear causal discovery methods.

BACKGROUND:  
Causal discovery from purely observational data often assumes robustness of combined linear/nonlinear CI tests to some level of hidden confounding. However, common evaluations using variable masking to simulate latent confounders conflate missing data effects with true latent confounding, leaving an open question about the baseline PC+KCI method’s robustness to *actual* latent variables that induce spurious dependencies. This gap is critical for applications in complex biological networks such as the Sachs dataset, where latent confounders are plausibly present.

APPROACH:  
Generate latent confounders explicitly by adding hidden common cause variables with controlled influence on observed nodes in the Sachs dataset (via data augmentation or generative modeling) rather than by masking observed variables. Apply the PC+KCI method on these augmented datasets with varying proportions of latent confounders and measure causal network reconstruction accuracy against the known ground truth using F1 score. Control for sample size and dimensionality by ensuring equal sample count and observed variable set across conditions.

EXPERIMENT:  
Use the Sachs protein signaling network dataset augmented with synthetic latent confounders modeled as hidden nodes influencing multiple observed variables with tunable strength and prevalence. Evaluate PC+KCI’s F1 score in recovering edges as latent confounder proportion increases from 0% to >40%, with a falsification threshold of F1 < 0.40 indicating substantial robustness failure.

NOVELTY:  
This study moves beyond ambiguous variable masking by explicitly modeling latent confounders and disentangling their effect from sample size or missing data artifacts, rigorously testing the baseline PC+KCI method’s true robustness. It provides the first quantitative threshold for performance degradation in nonlinear causal discovery under controlled latent confounding in a real biological dataset, guiding the development of improved latent-variable-aware methods.

topic: Causal discovery from observational data
text:
IDEA: Investigate whether applying PCMCI to segmented stationary and non-stationary intervals in real-world time series reveals substantial differences in causal graphs, falsifying the assumption of causal stability under non-stationarity.

BACKGROUND: Causal discovery methods for time series, including PCMCI, assume a stable causal structure over time, which often does not hold in real-world data exhibiting regime shifts or evolving dynamics. This assumption risks producing misleading causal inferences when the true causal graph changes, but existing work rarely quantifies the extent or impact of such violations. Addressing this gap is crucial for reliable causal inference in complex, temporally heterogeneous systems.

APPROACH: We segment publicly available time series datasets (UCI Electricity Load Diagrams, Yahoo Webscope S5) into stationary and non-stationary intervals using a rigorously pre-registered KPSS testing procedure with fixed window size, significance level, and preprocessing steps to ensure reproducibility and robustness. We then apply PCMCI separately on these intervals with matched sample sizes by downsampling or bootstrapping to control for power differences, and compare resulting graphs using Structural Hamming Distance (SHD). Additionally, we use permutation tests to control for distributional shifts unrelated to causal structure, isolating genuine structural changes.

EXPERIMENT: Run PCMCI on stationary vs. non-stationary segments of each dataset, compute SHD between inferred graphs, and assess if SHD exceeds a conservative 20% threshold of total possible edges, indicating sensitivity to non-stationarity. Validate segmentation robustness via sensitivity analysis over KPSS parameters, and control for sample size by equalizing data lengths per segment.

NOVELTY: This work rigorously quantifies the practical impact of violating causal stationarity assumptions on causal graph inference in real-world time series, explicitly controlling for confounds like sample size and distributional shifts—an advancement beyond prior nonlinear and deep-learning causal discovery methods that assume or overlook temporal causal stability.

topic: Deep learning emulators for climate model acceleration
text:
IDEA:  
Deep learning emulators trained solely on dynamic Smagorinsky model outputs exhibit quantifiable degradation in prediction accuracy, physical consistency, and coupled climate fidelity relative to the baseline dynamic Smagorinsky parameterization when deployed in fully coupled simulations, due to insufficient representation of true subgrid-scale variability in the training data.

BACKGROUND:  
Current deep learning emulators for subgrid-scale closures commonly rely exclusively on outputs from simplified physical models like the dynamic Smagorinsky closure, assuming that such data adequately represents subgrid processes for reliable coupled climate model deployment. However, this overlooks the complexity, nonlinear feedbacks, and state-dependent variability inherent in fully coupled climate systems, raising concerns that emulators trained on limited, idealized datasets may generalize poorly and induce biases or instabilities. Demonstrating the extent of this limitation is essential for guiding future emulator development and data sourcing strategies.

APPROACH:  
We train a convolutional neural network emulator on dynamic Smagorinsky subgrid flux outputs from the publicly available CESM Large Ensemble (CESM-LE) atmospheric column model data, capturing only the parameterization’s response under controlled conditions. The emulator then replaces the dynamic Smagorinsky model in short-term (e.g., 10-day) fully coupled CESM simulations. Evaluation employs normalized root mean square error (NRMSE) on subgrid flux predictions, near-surface temperature RMSE, plus additional diagnostics including spectral error metrics, total energy conservation checks, and stability indicators to rigorously assess physical consistency and numerical robustness.

EXPERIMENT:  
Use CESM-LE atmospheric column output to train the CNN emulator; then run short-term coupled CESM simulations with the emulator substituted for the dynamic Smagorinsky closure. Define failure as emulator subgrid flux NRMSE exceeding 20% relative to baseline and/or a >10% degradation in near-surface temperature RMSE, supplemented by any detected energy conservation violations or onset of numerical instabilities.

NOVELTY:  
Unlike prior work focused solely on offline or idealized settings, this experiment directly quantifies the emulator’s impact on fully coupled climate simulation fidelity with comprehensive, physically relevant diagnostics beyond aggregate error metrics. It isolates the fundamental limitation of relying exclusively on dynamic Smagorinsky outputs for training in realistic climate scenarios, providing a benchmark falsification threshold and public data baseline to rigorously challenge assumptions in deep learning parameterization emulation.

topic: Deep learning emulators for climate model acceleration
text:
IDEA:  
Evaluate the robustness of IPCC AR6 WGIII integrated assessment model (IAM) mitigation strategy projections by quantitatively comparing them to emission reduction outcomes from geographically and sectorally matched real-world pilot projects using standardized metrics and publicly available datasets.

BACKGROUND:  
IPCC AR6 WGIII scenarios synthesize state-of-the-art mitigation pathways using IAMs, forming the basis for climate policy and investment decisions. However, the degree to which these aggregated, model-based projections reliably reflect actual mitigation effectiveness at pilot-project scales remains untested, risking overconfidence in scenario-based policy frameworks.

APPROACH:  
We will harmonize mitigation effectiveness metrics—specifically, emissions reductions per standardized unit of capital expenditure and normalized carbon intensity changes—between IAM scenario baselines (e.g., MESSAGE and REMIND outputs from the IPCC data portal) and pilot project data drawn from CARMA and Climate Impact Lab. Rigorous normalization procedures and explicit spatial-temporal matching will control for scale and contextual confounders, ensuring comparability.

EXPERIMENT:  
Compare reported emissions reductions and carbon intensity improvements from ≥100 real-world mitigation pilot projects (2010–2020) against spatially and sectorally aligned IPCC AR6 WGIII IAM baseline projections, applying a falsification threshold of >20% relative difference to identify statistically significant deviations.

NOVELTY:  
This is the first systematic, metric-standardized validation of IPCC AR6 WGIII IAM mitigation projections against real-world pilot project outcomes at matched spatial and sectoral granularity, explicitly addressing common pitfalls of metric ambiguity, contextual confounding, and data representativeness that have limited prior empirical assessments.

topic: Deep learning emulators for climate model acceleration
text:
IDEA:  
Evaluate the out-of-distribution generalizability of deep learning emulators trained solely on dynamic Smagorinsky SGS tendencies from a single DYAMOND climate regime by benchmarking emulator mean squared error (MSE) against the baseline across distinct climate regimes, with a 10% MSE increase threshold defining generalization failure.

BACKGROUND:  
Deep learning emulators promise to accelerate climate model subgrid-scale parameterizations but rely on the assumption that training on SGS data from one climate regime can generalize to others. This assumption remains untested for fully coupled climate simulations; failure to generalize would limit practical deployment and necessitate new training or architectural strategies. Rigorous, quantitative evaluation of cross-regime emulator robustness is a critical gap in current climate ML research.

APPROACH:  
Train a convolutional neural network emulator exclusively on SGS tendencies generated by the dynamic Smagorinsky model within a well-defined DYAMOND tropical climate regime subset. Evaluate its performance by computing MSE on normalized SGS tendencies over spatiotemporal grids relative to the dynamic Smagorinsky outputs from two distinct DYAMOND extratropical regimes unseen during training, using the baseline model’s zero-error reference. Stability and physical consistency are inferred from comparable or degraded MSE values.

EXPERIMENT:  
Use publicly available DYAMOND high-resolution simulation data, training on SGS tendencies from the tropical regime for one week on a single GPU. Compute normalized SGS tendency MSE on held-out extratropical regimes, defining a 10% relative MSE increase over the baseline (dynamic Smagorinsky’s self-consistency) as failure to generalize.

NOVELTY:  
Unlike prior studies that focus on DL emulation within a single flow or regime and primarily reproduce training-distribution statistics, this work explicitly quantifies out-of-distribution generalization across multiple climate regimes in a fully coupled Earth system context, operationalizing a clear numeric threshold for success or failure relevant to practical climate model deployment.

topic: Deep learning emulators for climate model acceleration
text:
IDEA:  
Deep learning emulators trained solely on dynamic Smagorinsky LES data fail to reliably generalize in fully coupled climate model simulations, producing over 10% relative error in turbulent kinetic energy and density variance budgets, due to unresolved nonlinear feedbacks and stability issues.

BACKGROUND:  
Data-driven SGS closures have shown promise in replicating subgrid-scale turbulence in idealized LES settings, but their applicability in fully coupled climate models remains unproven. The nonlinear interactions and multiscale feedbacks in coupled Earth system simulations challenge the generalization and numerical stability of deep learning emulators trained on limited SGS parameterization data.

APPROACH:  
Train a deep neural network emulator exclusively on the DYAMOND LES dataset with the dynamic Smagorinsky closure as ground truth, carefully define and compute time- and domain-averaged kinetic energy and density variance budgets with explicit spatial and temporal filters, and replace the classical SGS scheme in a fully coupled climate model. Implement diagnostics to isolate spin-up transients by running control simulations with the original closure and enforce numerical stability through spectral norm regularization and energy-consistent constraints in the emulator.

EXPERIMENT:  
Use the publicly available DYAMOND LES dataset for training; evaluate emulator performance by embedding it in a well-documented coupled climate model (e.g., ICON or CESM) and measure relative errors in vertically integrated, monthly-averaged kinetic energy and density variance budgets compared to the dynamic Smagorinsky baseline, with a strict 10% error threshold defining success or failure.

NOVELTY:  
This study rigorously quantifies emulator generalization limits in fully coupled climate simulations using reproducible, physically interpretable metrics and isolates emulator-induced errors from model spin-up and coupling artifacts, addressing a critical gap overlooked in prior offline or idealized LES-only evaluations.

topic: Deep learning emulators for climate model acceleration
text:
IDEA:  
Deep neural network emulators trained exclusively on dynamic Smagorinsky model SGS fluxes fail to sustain long-term kinetic energy budget fidelity and dynamical stability in coupled climate model simulations, exposing fundamental limits of purely data-driven SGS parameter emulation.

BACKGROUND:  
Accurate subgrid-scale (SGS) parameterizations are critical for climate model fidelity but remain computationally expensive. While deep learning offers potential acceleration by emulating classical SGS models like the dynamic Smagorinsky closure, it is unresolved whether such emulators can maintain physical consistency—particularly energy conservation and stability—over extended coupled climate integrations. This addresses the gap in evaluating deep learning emulators beyond short-term, idealized tests towards fully coupled climate regimes.

APPROACH:  
Train a convolutional neural network (CNN) emulator solely on SGS fluxes generated by the dynamic Smagorinsky model from single-column or limited-area atmospheric simulations using publicly available CMIP6/CESM datasets. Integrate this emulator within a simplified coupled atmosphere-ocean model and run 30-day simulations, rigorously quantifying kinetic energy budget error as the time-averaged relative difference in vertically integrated kinetic energy dissipation rates compared to the baseline Smagorinsky model. Stability is defined as no exponential growth or blow-up in kinetic energy or state variables. A ≤5% time-averaged kinetic energy budget deviation after 30 days falsifies the hypothesis.

EXPERIMENT:  
Use CMIP6 single-column model data with dynamic Smagorinsky SGS fluxes for training; embed the trained CNN into the CESM atmosphere component coupled to a slab ocean; run 30-day simulations on a single GPU; compute the kinetic energy budget error as  
\[ \frac{1}{T} \int_0^T \left| \frac{D_{DNN}(t) - D_{SMAG}(t)}{D_{SMAG}(t)} \right| dt \]  
where \(D\) is the vertically integrated SGS kinetic energy dissipation rate, and \(T=30\) days.

NOVELTY:  
Unlike prior work focusing on short-term SGS flux emulation or offline skill, this study provides the first reproducible, quantitative evaluation of deep learning SGS emulators under fully coupled climate model feedbacks with a precisely defined, physically interpretable stability and energy budget metric. It directly tests the fundamental representativeness of dynamic Smagorinsky-based training data for deep emulators in operationally relevant multiday coupled scenarios.

topic: Energy-efficient neuromorphic computing
text:
IDEA:  
Quantitatively evaluate the impact of realistic neuromorphic workload-induced endurance degradation on memristor-based synapses by explicitly defining and counting physical switching events in simulation, and validating classification accuracy decay on the publicly available N-MNIST dataset against a stable non-degrading synapse baseline with a strict 10% accuracy drop threshold after one million switching cycles.

BACKGROUND:  
Memristor devices show promising endurance in controlled lab experiments, but it remains unclear if their long-term switching stability holds under realistic neuromorphic workloads characterized by correlated weight updates and stochastic spike timing. Prior device studies often conflate algorithmic weight changes with physical switching events, lacking clear operational definitions and controls to isolate device endurance effects from network or training instabilities, which limits confidence in their system-level robustness.

APPROACH:  
Implement a memristor synapse model from Wang et al. (2018) in a spiking neural network simulation with a rigorously defined synaptic update as a physical switching event above a specified conductance change threshold, directly comparable to device endurance metrics. Run two parallel experiments on the N-MNIST dataset: one with endurance degradation modeled and another idealized non-degrading synapse, measuring classification accuracy after exactly one million physical switching cycles per synapse to isolate endurance effects.

EXPERIMENT:  
Train and evaluate a spiking neural network on the N-MNIST dataset using the Wang et al. memristor model; count physical switching events as synaptic updates when conductance changes exceed a defined threshold aligned with device switching, stopping at one million updates per synapse; measure classification accuracy degradation relative to the idealized non-degrading baseline, test for >10% drop as the falsification criterion.

NOVELTY:  
This work uniquely bridges device-level endurance definitions with system-level neuromorphic workload simulations through explicit, reproducible switching event counting and baseline controls, directly testing the endurance-performance relationship under realistic conditions rather than relying on idealized or algorithmic update proxies common in prior studies.

topic: Energy-efficient neuromorphic computing
text:
IDEA:  
Thermal fluctuations and device variability in multi-device organic HTSP arrays cause nonlinear degradation of synaptic accuracy in neuromorphic SNNs, disproving assumptions that single-device thermal stability guarantees circuit-level robustness.

BACKGROUND:  
While organic high-temperature synaptic phototransistors (HTSPs) demonstrate strong thermal stability at the isolated device level, their behavior under realistic multi-device integration and fluctuating thermal conditions remains unquantified. Existing studies overlook thermal cross-talk and fabrication-induced variability effects that could destabilize synaptic function and degrade neuromorphic network accuracy in harsh environments.

APPROACH:  
We will extend the Diehl & Cook (2015) spiking neural network baseline trained on the publicly available N-MNIST dataset by incorporating experimentally calibrated thermal fluctuation profiles and measured device parameter variability into both training and inference simulations. Thermal noise models will be derived from empirical thermal cycling data on HTSP arrays, capturing spatial-temporal non-uniformities and cross-talk, ensuring accurate representation of multi-device thermal dynamics.

EXPERIMENT:  
Accuracy degradation under combined thermal noise and device variability will be quantified by training and testing the SNN with these perturbations; a >5% accuracy drop relative to the baseline will confirm synaptic instability at the system level. Thermal profiles will be experimentally validated prior to simulation to ensure fidelity.

NOVELTY:  
This is the first study to integrate empirically validated multi-device thermal fluctuation and device variability models into neuromorphic SNN simulations, rigorously testing the scalability of single-device HTSP thermal stability claims to circuit-level operation, thereby bridging the gap between device physics and system-level neuromorphic performance.

topic: Energy-efficient neuromorphic computing
text:
IDEA:  
Organic high-temperature synaptic phototransistors exhibit significant (>10%) degradation in synaptic response accuracy and energy efficiency under variable temperature and humidity cycling compared to constant high-temperature operation, challenging the assumption of their robust environmental stability.

BACKGROUND:  
While prior studies demonstrate stable synaptic function of organic phototransistors at constant elevated temperatures (e.g., 85°C), real-world neuromorphic systems encounter dynamic and cyclic environmental stresses including humidity fluctuations that may induce reversible and irreversible device changes. Current models overlook these realistic environmental variations, leaving open the question of whether such conditions degrade synaptic performance and energy efficiency in integrated neuromorphic tasks.

APPROACH:  
We simulate a spiking neural network (SNN) trained with spike-timing-dependent plasticity (STDP) on the publicly available N-MNIST dataset, using a validated device-level model of organic phototransistor synapses subjected to controlled temperature and humidity cycling versus a constant 85°C baseline. Synaptic plasticity changes are isolated by normalizing photoresponse signals to baseline drift and sensor noise through interleaved recovery periods, ensuring hysteresis and reversible effects are decoupled from true degradation.

EXPERIMENT:  
Measure classification accuracy and normalized energy consumption after 1000 cycles of variable temperature (25°C–85°C) and humidity (20%–80% RH) against a constant 85°C baseline, declaring >10% relative performance loss as significant degradation; device noise and drift are accounted for by post-cycle recovery measurements and baseline correction protocols.

NOVELTY:  
This is the first study to rigorously quantify the impact of combined variable temperature and humidity cycling on organic phototransistor synaptic function within a realistic neuromorphic learning framework, explicitly controlling for reversible hysteresis effects and sensor noise, thereby providing critical insights beyond prior constant-temperature evaluations and purely hardware-characterization-focused work.

topic: Energy-efficient neuromorphic computing
text:
IDEA:  
Large-scale memristor-based neuromorphic networks will exhibit more than 10% sustained accuracy degradation on N-MNIST over 10^6 inference cycles due to cumulative device variability and instability not predicted by existing small-scale dynamic reconfiguration models.

BACKGROUND:  
While small-scale memristor devices demonstrate stable analog neural emulation under controlled conditions, their real-world scalability remains unverified, particularly regarding variability and temporal instability effects. Current models assume that device-level fluctuations average out or are compensable, but these assumptions lack rigorous validation in large, operational neuromorphic systems over extended durations.

APPROACH:  
We deploy the established dynamic memristor reconfiguration baseline model on a spiking neural network trained on the publicly available N-MNIST dataset, rigorously evaluating classification accuracy at fixed intervals over 10^6 continuous inference cycles at controlled temperature (25±1°C) and voltage conditions. Accuracy measurements occur every 10^4 cycles without retraining or calibration, with control runs on a non-memristive digital baseline to isolate device-specific degradation from software or data drift.

EXPERIMENT:  
Train the baseline memristor-model neuromorphic network on N-MNIST, then repeatedly test accuracy every 10,000 inference cycles for a total of one million cycles under stable environmental and electrical conditions, defining degradation as a sustained >10% drop from initial accuracy without recalibration or retraining.

NOVELTY:  
This experiment explicitly addresses temporal and scale-related instability in memristor arrays using a tightly controlled, reproducible protocol that isolates device degradation from systemic confounds, directly challenging the untested assumption of linear scalability in prior small-scale models and providing the first quantitative long-term performance limits for memristor-based neuromorphic computing.

topic: Energy-efficient neuromorphic computing
text:
IDEA:  
Quantitatively evaluate the impact of long-term endurance and variability degradation in memristor-based synapses on system-level energy efficiency and accuracy using a rigorously calibrated simulation model validated against short-term empirical data and realistic neuromorphic workloads.

BACKGROUND:  
Current neuromorphic computing research assumes memristor synapse endurance and variability remain stable under extended, realistic workloads, based largely on short-term lab tests or idealized models. This untested assumption risks underestimating degradation effects that could critically impair network accuracy and energy efficiency in practical deployments. Establishing whether synaptic device aging meaningfully degrades system performance under realistic continuous operation remains an open problem.

APPROACH:  
Simulate a spiking neural network with Differential Pair Integrator (DPI) synapses augmented by memristor device models explicitly calibrated against measured short-term endurance and variability data from state-of-the-art devices. Apply a workload of 1 million synaptic updates using the publicly available N-MNIST dataset and realistic spike train statistics to track cumulative degradation effects on classification accuracy and per-inference energy consumption. Validate the device-level memristor parameters experimentally before simulation to ensure physical fidelity and isolate device degradation from algorithmic instability.

EXPERIMENT:  
Run the spiking network simulation on N-MNIST with memristor dynamics over 1 million synaptic updates; measure accuracy drop and energy increase relative to baseline short-term operation. Confirm the hypothesis if accuracy degrades by more than 10% or energy consumption per inference rises by more than 20%.

NOVELTY:  
This work uniquely integrates empirically validated memristor endurance and variability data into long-duration neuromorphic workload simulations, directly addressing the gap between short-term device characterization and realistic system-level impact. Unlike prior studies, it rigorously separates device degradation effects from model artifacts and employs a workload complexity reflective of practical neuromorphic scenarios, providing the first reproducible quantitative threshold for endurance-driven performance decay.

topic: Generative AI for drug discovery and molecular design
text:
IDEA:  
Quantitatively evaluate whether augmenting global molecular datasets with indigenous Nigerian medicinal plant data significantly improves chemical diversity and drug-likeness of molecules generated by fine-tuned MolGPT, using multi-faceted diversity metrics and rigorously controlled fine-tuning.

BACKGROUND:  
It is widely assumed that incorporating indigenous natural product data into generative AI models enriches chemical diversity and drug-likeness of generated compounds, due to unique local chemotypes. However, this assumption remains untested in a controlled manner, especially given that state-of-the-art models pretrained on massive global datasets may already capture broad chemical space, potentially diminishing the impact of smaller indigenous datasets. This study directly challenges the presumed additive value of local data for generative molecular design.

APPROACH:  
We fine-tune the pretrained MolGPT model separately on the ZINC15 dataset alone and on a combined dataset of ZINC15 plus AfroDB (containing curated Nigerian medicinal plant molecules), carefully balancing data representation and optimizing fine-tuning hyperparameters to ensure meaningful model adaptation. To address the limitations of single metrics, we evaluate generated molecules using multiple complementary metrics: Shannon entropy of Morgan fingerprints, Bemis-Murcko scaffold counts, Tanimoto diversity distributions, and median QED scores, providing a robust assessment of chemical novelty and predicted drug-likeness.

EXPERIMENT:  
From each fine-tuned model, generate 10,000 molecules; compare chemical diversity and drug-likeness between models, defining a priori a 5% relative improvement threshold in any metric as significant. Use only publicly available datasets (ZINC15 and AfroDB), the openly available MolGPT baseline, and reproducible fine-tuning protocols to ensure immediate replicability.

NOVELTY:  
Unlike prior work that assumes indigenous datasets inherently enhance generative models or relies on a single diversity metric, this study rigorously tests that assumption with controlled fine-tuning, multiple orthogonal diversity measures, and explicit statistical thresholds, providing the first quantitative benchmark of indigenous African natural product data’s true impact on state-of-the-art generative molecular design.

topic: Generative AI for drug discovery and molecular design
text:
IDEA:  
Integrating localized Nigerian medicinal plant data with global molecular databases in training generative AI models reduces generalizability by biasing outputs toward local chemotypes, resulting in significant declines in multi-metric drug-likeness and diversity benchmarks compared to global-only trained models.

BACKGROUND:
