Current drug discovery generative AI research assumes that adding localized datasets to global molecular data uniformly enhances chemical diversity and model performance. However, the potential for domain shift causing overfitting to localized chemotypes and degradation in broadly-applicable drug-likeness remains unquantified, particularly for African natural product data like AfroDB. Addressing this gap is critical for designing balanced datasets that maximize generalizable drug discovery outcomes.

APPROACH:  
Train the MolGPT autoregressive transformer model on (1) the global ZINC15 dataset alone and (2) a balanced merged dataset combining AfroDB (Nigerian medicinal plants) and ZINC15 with carefully controlled local-to-global ratios. Evaluate generated molecules on multiple complementary metrics—QED, synthetic accessibility (SA) score, scaffold diversity (Bemis–Murcko scaffolds), and physicochemical property distributions—to robustly characterize model generalizability and bias. Control for dataset size and distribution by stratified sampling to ensure AfroDB compounds represent ~20% of training data in merged sets.

EXPERIMENT:  
Train MolGPT with fixed hyperparameters on (a) ZINC15-only baseline and (b) AfroDB+ZINC15 merged dataset; generate 10,000 molecules per model and benchmark on held-out ZINC test set. Define falsification thresholds as >10% decrease in average QED, >5% worsening in SA score, and >10% reduction in scaffold diversity relative to baseline, collectively indicating reduced generalizability due to local data integration.

NOVELTY:  
This study uniquely tests localized African natural product integration effects on generative model generalizability using a multi-metric evaluation framework and rigorous dataset balancing, revealing potential pitfalls of naïve dataset merging overlooked by prior work focused on global or local datasets in isolation. It also provides actionable insights for domain adaptation and dataset curation strategies in AI-driven drug design.

topic: Generative AI for drug discovery and molecular design
text:
IDEA:  
Assess whether integrating indigenous Nigerian medicinal plant data from AfroDb with global ChEMBL datasets significantly improves the drug-likeness and predicted bioactivity of molecules generated by modern generative AI models, using rigorous dataset balancing and multiple validated metrics.

BACKGROUND:  
Current literature assumes that including region-specific indigenous molecular data enhances generative AI outputs for drug discovery, but this remains unproven under controlled conditions. Existing studies often overlook dataset size imbalance, chemical diversity overlap, and reliance on limited metrics, leaving open whether indigenous data provides meaningful additive value beyond large global datasets.

APPROACH:  
We will train two generative models—an ORGAN baseline and a state-of-the-art transformer-based model with reinforcement learning—on (1) ChEMBL alone and (2) a carefully curated, size-matched ChEMBL plus AfroDb combined dataset with chemical space stratification. Generated molecules will be evaluated using multiple complementary metrics: Quantitative Estimate of Drug-likeness (QED), synthetic accessibility, scaffold novelty, and predicted bioactivity scores from validated ML classifiers and consensus docking to orthogonal targets, ensuring robustness beyond heuristic proxies.

EXPERIMENT:  
Train the ORGAN and transformer models on (a) ChEMBL only (baseline) and (b) ChEMBL plus AfroDb balanced by chemical diversity and size; compare generated molecule sets for a ≥10% increase in mean QED or ≥15% increase in predicted bioactivity probability against baseline, using publicly available datasets (ChEMBL v29, AfroDb) and open-source tools (RDKit, AutoDock Vina, pretrained bioactivity ML models).

NOVELTY:  
This study explicitly counters prior assumptions by controlling for dataset imbalance, employing multiple generative model architectures, and integrating orthogonal evaluation metrics to rigorously quantify the true added value of indigenous Nigerian medicinal data in AI-driven molecular design—clarifying its practical impact and guiding future data integration strategies.

topic: Generative AI for drug discovery and molecular design
text:
IDEA: Deep generative models such as JT-VAE require rigorously optimized, task-specific adaptation—including domain-aware metrics and fine-tuning—to achieve practical validity, novelty, and drug-likeness thresholds in molecular generation, refuting assumptions that default, out-of-the-box models suffice.

BACKGROUND: While deep generative models like VAEs, GANs, transformers, and DDPMs show theoretical promise for molecular design, the field often assumes these architectures transfer effectively to drug discovery tasks without substantial modification. However, practical deployment demands molecules that are not only chemically valid but also drug-like, synthetically accessible, and scaffold-diverse—criteria often unmet by default models trained on generic datasets. This gap challenges the assumption that large-scale training alone ensures applicability in real-world pipelines.

APPROACH: We establish a rigorously optimized baseline by training a JT-VAE on the ZINC250K dataset with hyperparameters tuned via grid search and early stopping to ensure stable convergence. We evaluate generated molecules using domain-relevant metrics: chemical validity (≥95%), scaffold novelty (≥75%, measured by Bemis-Murcko scaffold distinctness), synthetic accessibility score (SAS ≤ 3.5 for ≥80% of outputs), and quantitative estimate of drug-likeness (QED ≥ 0.5 for ≥70%). If the baseline fails these thresholds, we apply task-specific adaptations including reinforcement learning to optimize ADMET-related rewards and hybrid graph-transformer architectures to improve scaffold diversity and drug-likeness.

EXPERIMENT: Baseline JT-VAE training on ZINC250K with optimized hyperparameters evaluated against multi-dimensional metrics (validity, scaffold novelty, SAS, QED) with preset thresholds: validity ≥95%, scaffold novelty ≥75%, SAS ≤3.5 for 80% molecules, and QED ≥0.5 for 70%. Follow-up adaptations tested to quantify improvements over baseline.

NOVELTY: This work advances beyond prior studies by integrating rigorous baseline optimization with domain-specific validity, novelty, and drug-likeness metrics, directly addressing confounds of prior assessments and clearly quantifying the necessity and impact of task-specific adaptations in generative AI for drug discovery.

topic: Generative AI for drug discovery and molecular design
text:
IDEA:  
Specialized generative AI architectures incorporating indigenous plant chemistry-aware embeddings and graph neural modules outperform baseline REINVENT 4 models trained on combined AfroDB and ZINC15 datasets by generating molecules with significantly higher predicted bioactivity (pIC50 ≥ 7.0) against Nigerian region-specific therapeutic targets.

BACKGROUND:  
Global generative models like REINVENT 4 are typically trained on large, diverse molecular databases but may inadequately capture the unique chemical features of indigenous Nigerian medicinal plants, limiting their effectiveness for region-specific drug discovery. Current approaches often assume dataset augmentation alone suffices, neglecting potential architectural mismatches with underrepresented local chemical spaces. This gap risks generating molecules with suboptimal predicted efficacy against local disease targets, a critical challenge for equitable AI-driven drug discovery.

APPROACH:  
We propose augmenting the baseline REINVENT 4 architecture with domain-specific embedding layers encoding indigenous natural product structural motifs and integrating graph neural network (GNN) modules tailored to capture the complex stereochemistry and scaffolding prevalent in AfroDB compounds. This hybrid model will be trained on a combined AfroDB and ZINC15 dataset and optimized using reinforcement learning targeting experimentally validated predictive models for region-specific targets. Predictive models will be rigorously validated on held-out AfroDB compounds to ensure bioactivity predictions reflect indigenous chemistry.

EXPERIMENT:  
Train baseline REINVENT 4 and the adapted model on the merged AfroDB (Nigerian medicinal plants) and ZINC15 dataset with balanced sampling to prevent bias. Evaluate generated molecules using a validated pIC50 prediction model fine-tuned on AfroDB for Nigerian therapeutic targets, defining successful generation as molecules with average predicted pIC50 ≥ 7.0. Statistical significance between models will be assessed via bootstrapped confidence intervals on bioactivity and novelty metrics.

NOVELTY:  
This work uniquely combines architectural customization—embedding indigenous chemical knowledge and GNN modules—with stringent predictive model validation rooted in region-specific bioactivity data, directly addressing dataset bias and prediction ambiguity critiques. It advances beyond prior studies by explicitly testing and quantifying the necessity of architectural adaptation for underrepresented local molecular spaces, offering a replicable framework for tailored generative AI in decentralized drug discovery.

topic: Uncertainty quantification in deep neural networks
text:
IDEA: Evaluate whether uncertainty quantification methods—including Bayesian Neural Networks, Monte Carlo Dropout, ensembles, and Gaussian Processes—provide at least a 10% reduction in safety-critical failure rates on autonomous driving tasks with rigorously defined failure metrics under realistic, publicly available datasets.

BACKGROUND: While UQ methods are theoretically motivated to improve model reliability by better capturing predictive uncertainty, it remains unverified if these theoretical benefits translate into meaningful safety improvements in real-world autonomous driving scenarios. Existing work lacks standardized, quantifiable safety metrics tied to operational failure modes and often overlooks confounding factors such as model calibration and dataset biases.

APPROACH: We will implement well-established UQ methods (BNNs, MC Dropout, ensembles, GPs) on a state-of-the-art object detection or trajectory prediction model trained on publicly available datasets (starting with nuScenes). Failure modes will be simulated through controlled, realistic perturbations—sensor noise, occlusions, and adversarial attacks—with a clearly defined failure event metric (e.g., collision prediction errors or false negative detection rate) linked explicitly to safety outcomes. Statistical controls including matched deterministic baselines and training protocols will isolate the impact of uncertainty estimation from factors like regularization or ensembling effects.

EXPERIMENT: The minimal experiment uses nuScenes for object detection or prediction, applying MC Dropout to generate uncertainty estimates. We measure failure rates as the fraction of safety-critical errors (e.g., missed detections causing potential collisions) under simulated perturbations and require at least a 10% relative reduction compared to a deterministic baseline. Follow-up experiments scale to Waymo Open Dataset and Argoverse 2 and compare all UQ methods under identical conditions.

NOVELTY: This study rigorously operationalizes safety-critical failure metrics and isolates uncertainty quantification effects from confounds, providing the first large-scale empirical benchmark that directly tests whether theoretically superior UQ methods yield practically meaningful safety improvements in realistic autonomous driving scenarios.

topic: Uncertainty quantification in deep neural networks
text:
IDEA:  
Evaluate and compare the robustness of Bhattacharyya coefficient-based uncertainty quantification against Monte Carlo Dropout on standardized out-of-distribution (SVHN) and adversarial (FGSM, ε=8/255, untargeted) examples using calibrated metrics to determine if the Bhattacharyya method underperforms with AUROC < 0.75 for anomaly detection.

BACKGROUND:  
Uncertainty quantification (UQ) is vital for reliable deep neural network deployment in safety-critical tasks, yet the robustness of recently proposed Bhattacharyya coefficient-based UQ beyond in-distribution classification remains unclear. Existing work largely evaluates such methods on in-distribution data, leaving open whether distributional overlap metrics maintain reliability under distribution shifts and adversarial attacks.

APPROACH:  
Train a standard CNN on CIFAR-10 with carefully tuned hyperparameters separately optimized for Bhattacharyya coefficient and MC Dropout to ensure fair comparison. Evaluate both methods on aligned, preprocessed SVHN OOD samples and FGSM adversarial attacks (ε=8/255, untargeted, single-step), reporting AUROC for detection alongside expected calibration error and decision threshold sensitivity to capture uncertainty quality comprehensively.

EXPERIMENT:  
Use CIFAR-10 for training, SVHN as OOD (resized and normalized identically to CIFAR-10), and generate FGSM adversarial examples on CIFAR-10 test set with ε=8/255 untargeted attack; compute AUROC for OOD and adversarial detection, flagging Bhattacharyya method’s AUROC < 0.75 as evidence of degraded robustness compared to MC Dropout under identical training and evaluation protocols.

NOVELTY:  
This study rigorously controls preprocessing, hyperparameter tuning, and evaluation metrics to isolate inherent robustness differences, addressing gaps in prior work that lack standardized OOD/adversarial benchmarks and calibration analysis for Bhattacharyya coefficient-based UQ methods. The approach bridges theoretical appeal with practical deployment challenges, providing the first calibrated robustness comparison on publicly available datasets.

topic: Uncertainty quantification in deep neural networks
text:
IDEA:  
Evaluate whether Bhattacharyya coefficient weighting in MC dropout improves uncertainty quantification by increasing predictive entropy on out-of-distribution and adversarial inputs beyond a 10% relative increase compared to standard MC dropout.

BACKGROUND:  
Uncertainty quantification in deep neural networks is critical for safe deployment, especially under distributional shifts and adversarial attacks. Although Bhattacharyya coefficient weighting has been proposed to enhance MC dropout by penalizing distributional overlap, its practical effect on uncertainty estimates for OOD and adversarial examples remains insufficiently validated and may lead to overconfident predictions.

APPROACH:  
Implement Bhattacharyya coefficient weighting as a per-sample scalar factor applied to the predictive distribution from MC dropout by reweighting dropout sample probabilities before calculating predictive entropy. Compare this to baseline MC dropout on a standard CNN trained on CIFAR-10 by measuring predictive entropy on CIFAR-10 test (in-distribution), CIFAR-100 (OOD), and FGSM adversarial examples generated with fixed ε=0.03, ensuring reproducibility. A 10% relative increase in entropy on OOD and adversarial samples is the threshold for improved uncertainty quantification.

EXPERIMENT:  
Train a standard CNN with MC dropout on CIFAR-10; evaluate predictive entropy on CIFAR-10 test, CIFAR-100, and FGSM (ε=0.03) adversarial samples. Compare entropy between baseline MC dropout and Bhattacharyya-weighted MC dropout, using publicly available datasets and code for MC dropout. Confirm statistical significance with multiple seeds (≥5).

NOVELTY:  
This is the first rigorously controlled empirical test with well-defined Bhattacharyya coefficient integration and a numeric falsification threshold on a standard benchmark that explicitly challenges recent positive claims, addressing prior ambiguity in weighting implementation and adversarial strength while establishing reproducible methodology.

topic: Uncertainty quantification in deep neural networks
text:
IDEA: Neural network regularization methods for uncertainty quantification in full-waveform inversion systematically fail to maintain calibration robustness when tested on controlled noisy and geologically complex variants of SEAM Phase I data, quantifiably increasing Expected Calibration Error beyond 10%.

BACKGROUND: While Bayesian neural networks (BNNs) in full-waveform inversion (FWI) leverage spatial correlations to regularize uncertainty estimates, their robustness under realistic noise levels and complex geologies remains unverified. Existing literature implicitly assumes that these spatial priors generalize across data conditions, but domain shifts introduced by noise and geological heterogeneity could undermine uncertainty calibration, limiting practical deployment in geophysics.

APPROACH: We propose to train a BNN-based FWI model (Mosser et al., 2019) exclusively on noise-free SEAM Phase I data and evaluate uncertainty calibration on systematically generated test sets with precisely quantified noise (SNR 5–20 dB) and geological complexity metrics (e.g., interface roughness, velocity contrast). Expected Calibration Error (ECE) will be computed with bootstrap confidence intervals across repeated trials to ensure statistical significance.

EXPERIMENT: Using publicly available SEAM Phase I synthetic data, we generate noisy and geologically complex variants through reproducible perturbation protocols, then measure ECE of the BNN UQ method on these variants versus noise-free baseline; a falsification threshold of >10% relative ECE increase confirms failure of the spatial correlation prior to robustly regularize uncertainty.

NOVELTY: This work explicitly quantifies the breakdown of neural network spatial regularization for uncertainty quantification in FWI under rigorously controlled domain shifts, addressing a critical gap overlooked by prior studies that assume robustness without systematic testing on noise and complexity; the combination of reproducible complexity metrics, statistical calibration rigor, and clear falsification criteria distinguishes this research.

topic: Uncertainty quantification in deep neural networks
text:
IDEA:  
Evaluate whether standard uncertainty quantification methods in deep neural networks maintain calibration and robustness under realistic distributional shifts and continual learning, using multiple complementary metrics and well-controlled continual adaptation protocols.

BACKGROUND:  
While many UQ methods demonstrate strong calibration on standard benchmarks like CIFAR-10, their reliability under realistic deployment conditions involving distributional shifts and continual learning remains unclear. Existing evaluations often rely on single metrics (ECE) and synthetic corruption datasets, which may misrepresent true robustness and conflate uncertainty degradation with model retraining failures. This work addresses the critical gap between benchmark performance and real-world UQ reliability.

APPROACH:  
We apply Monte Carlo Dropout as a baseline to assess uncertainty calibration and robustness using multiple metrics (Expected Calibration Error, Negative Log-Likelihood, Brier Score, and out-of-distribution detection AUC) under CIFAR-10-C/100-C corruptions and Split CIFAR-100 continual learning, incorporating explicit retraining protocols to isolate uncertainty failures from catastrophic forgetting. Controlled continual learning setups will retrain models with fixed UQ methods to ensure measured degradation stems from UQ limitations rather than adaptation artifacts.

EXPERIMENT:  
Run inference with MC Dropout on CIFAR-10-C and CIFAR-100-C, measuring ECE, NLL, Brier score, and OOD detection AUC; then perform continual learning on Split CIFAR-100 with careful model retraining and evaluate the same metrics after each task. A falsification threshold is defined as ≤5% relative increase in ECE and NLL compared to IID baseline, combined with stable OOD detection performance, indicating robust uncertainty quantification.

NOVELTY:  
This study rigorously controls for confounding factors in continual learning and employs a multi-metric evaluation framework, providing the first systematic validation of whether benchmark-successful UQ methods truly generalize to practical deployment scenarios involving realistic shifts and adaptation, beyond prior work focused on single metrics or synthetic corruptions alone.

topic: Scaling laws for Large Language Models
text:
IDEA: Adaptive curriculum-based mixing of general and domain-specific corpora during continual pre-training dynamically shifts the data ratio to improve domain task performance beyond fixed-ratio baselines.

BACKGROUND: Prior work like the D-CPT Law (2024) identifies fixed optimal mixture ratios for continual pre-training on domain corpora, assuming static data blending suffices. However, it remains unclear if a static ratio best supports evolving model learning needs across training phases, especially as models progress from general understanding to domain specialization.

APPROACH: We propose an adaptive curriculum that starts with a high proportion of general-corpus data and gradually increases domain-specific data based on domain validation perplexity trends, controlling for total training tokens to ensure fair comparison. This dynamic schedule aims to scaffold learning by aligning data mixture with the model’s shifting domain knowledge acquisition.

EXPERIMENT: Continual pre-train a LLaMA-small model on a fixed 70/30 OpenWebText-to-PubMed OA mixture baseline versus the adaptive curriculum schedule, matched for total tokens and training compute; evaluate on held-out biomedical benchmarks using perplexity, requiring at least a 2% perplexity reduction over baseline sustained across three independent runs to confirm hypothesis.

NOVELTY: Unlike prior fixed-ratio CPT approaches, this method introduces an explicitly adaptive and scaffolded data mixing curriculum driven by domain validation signals, rigorously controlled for training budget to isolate curriculum effects, thereby testing a fundamental assumption about static vs. dynamic data blending in CPT for LLMs.

topic: Scaling laws for Large Language Models
text:
IDEA: Adaptive mixture ratio schedules that dynamically adjust the proportion of general and domain-specific data during continual pre-training improve validation perplexity by at least 1.5% over fixed, grid-searched mixture ratios while maintaining controlled corpus exposure and stable training dynamics.

BACKGROUND: Selecting a fixed mixture ratio between general and domain-specific corpora for continual pre-training of LLMs is costly due to exhaustive grid search and may be suboptimal across training stages. Current methods assume static mixture ratios best balance general linguistic representation and domain expertise, ignoring potential benefits from dynamic adaptation guided by validation feedback.

APPROACH: We propose an adaptive mixture scheduling algorithm that updates data sampling proportions based on smoothed validation perplexity trends on a held-out biomedical set, with explicit constraints to equalize total token exposure to each corpus relative to fixed baselines. This controls for confounds related to training dynamics and prevents oscillations by applying exponential moving averages and minimum dwell times before ratio updates.

EXPERIMENT: Fine-tune GPT-2 small for one epoch on a mixture of OpenWebText2 and PubMed Abstracts, comparing the adaptive schedule to the best fixed mixture ratio found via grid search, using held-out biomedical validation perplexity as the metric. Success is a statistically significant ≥1.5% perplexity reduction on a separate held-out test biomedical set, ensuring results generalize beyond the validation subset and avoid overfitting.

NOVELTY: This work uniquely combines adaptive mixture scheduling with rigorous exposure control and stability mechanisms to overcome known pitfalls of dynamic data balancing, differentiating it from prior grid-search-dependent or static-ratio methods, and addressing limitations highlighted by the D-CPT Law and related scaling studies.

topic: Scaling laws for Large Language Models
text:
IDEA: Adaptive mixture ratio schedules that dynamically adjust the balance between domain-specific and general-domain data during continual pre-training based on a stable, domain-specific validation perplexity improve downstream domain task performance compared to fixed-ratio baselines.

BACKGROUND: Current domain-specific continual pre-training (CPT) of LLMs relies on costly manual grid searches to select fixed mixture ratios of general and domain data, which may be suboptimal and inefficient. There is an unresolved challenge in automating data mixture scheduling to improve domain adaptation without inducing instability or catastrophic forgetting.

APPROACH: We propose an adaptive scheduling algorithm that adjusts the mixture ratio every fixed interval of training steps by monitoring domain-specific perplexity on a clean, held-out validation set balanced exclusively on the domain corpus. The schedule increases domain data proportion if perplexity improves and decreases it when perplexity plateaus or degrades, with safeguards to prevent abrupt ratio swings and ensure total training steps and domain token exposure match the fixed baseline.

EXPERIMENT: Using the GPT-2 small model, we will continually pre-train on a 50/50 fixed baseline mixture of PubMed Central Open Access and Wikipedia data versus the adaptive schedule variant, with validation perplexity computed every 2,000 steps on a held-out PubMed validation set. Final evaluation is on a PubMed classification downstream task fine-tuned equally from both CPT checkpoints; an adaptive schedule is considered successful if it yields ≥2% lower validation loss than the fixed baseline averaged over 3 runs.

NOVELTY: Unlike prior work that conducts costly fixed-ratio grid searches or ignores stable validation criteria during scheduling, this method uses a principled, domain-specific perplexity metric and strict compute/data exposure normalization to enable robust, data-driven mixture ratio adaptation, marking a first controlled demonstration of adaptive CPT schedules for improved domain-specific LLM tuning.

topic: Scaling laws for Large Language Models
text:
IDEA:  
The optimal mixture ratio between general and domain-specific corpora during continual pre-training varies systematically with model scale and compute budget, invalidating the fixed-ratio baseline from Gururangan et al. (2020).

BACKGROUND:  
Current continual pre-training protocols assume a single, fixed optimal mixture ratio of general to domain data applies universally across model scales, based on prior empirical findings. However, emerging evidence on model scaling laws suggests that learning dynamics and data utility shift with model capacity and compute constraints, raising the question of whether mixture ratios should be scale- and compute-dependent. Resolving this uncertainty is critical for effective, cost-efficient domain adaptation of large language models.

APPROACH:  
We conduct controlled continual pre-training of transformer models at two distinct scales (~125M and ~355M parameters) using The Pile as general data and PubMed Central Open Access as domain-specific biomedical data. We perform a fine-grained grid search over mixture ratios (0% to 100% domain data in 5% increments) with multiple random seeds, evaluating each checkpoint on held-out biomedical validation sets using domain perplexity and downstream biomedical task metrics. Training runs employ early stopping based on validation convergence to ensure comparable optimization across scales.

EXPERIMENT:  
Identify the optimal mixture ratio per model scale as the ratio yielding the lowest domain perplexity averaged over three seeds, with a >5% absolute difference between scales falsifying the fixed-ratio baseline. The minimal experiment uses publicly available datasets and the Gururangan et al. (2020) fixed ratio (~25% domain data) as baseline. Statistical significance is tested with bootstrap confidence intervals to confirm differences are robust beyond random noise.

NOVELTY:  
This work rigorously quantifies scale- and compute-dependent shifts in data mixture ratios for continual pre-training, challenging a widely assumed fixed-ratio protocol. Unlike prior grid-search-heavy or single-scale studies, it explicitly controls for convergence and noise, providing the first statistically powered evidence that mixture ratio is a critical hyperparameter scaling with model capacity and compute budget.

topic: Scaling laws for Large Language Models
text:
IDEA: Architectural variations in attention mechanisms and normalization layers systematically alter the scaling laws of Transformer language models, producing statistically significant deviations from baseline power-law loss trends beyond width and depth effects.

BACKGROUND: Current scaling law research (Kaplan et al., 2020) asserts that language model loss scales predictably with model size and dataset size, largely independent of micro-architectural details beyond width and depth. This leaves open whether finer architectural design choices—such as alternative attention mechanisms or normalization schemes—can meaningfully shift these scaling relationships, a question unresolved due to limited controlled experimentation and statistical rigor.

APPROACH: We will train controlled families of Transformer models on WikiText-103, systematically varying attention types (standard self-attention, linear, sparse, dynamic) and normalization layers (LayerNorm, RMSNorm, and recent alternatives), while controlling hyperparameters per variant through small targeted sweeps to ensure stable convergence. We will fit power-law curves to validation loss versus model size across at least five model scales (10M–200M parameters), applying bootstrap confidence intervals to baseline fits to robustly quantify deviations.

EXPERIMENT: The minimal experiment trains five model sizes × four attention variants × three normalization variants on WikiText-103, measuring validation cross-entropy loss curves and comparing power-law fits using RMSE with a >5% deviation threshold outside the 95% confidence interval of baseline fits indicating meaningful architectural effects.

NOVELTY: Unlike prior scaling law studies focusing on width, depth, or compute, this work rigorously isolates and statistically validates the impact of micro-architectural variants on scaling behavior, using controlled hyperparameter tuning and probabilistic fit assessments to overcome noise and fitting ambiguity, thus extending scaling law understanding beyond coarse architectural parameters.

topic: Emergent communication in multi-agent systems
text:
IDEA:  
Template transfer training of compositional communication protocols does not scale effectively from dyadic referential tasks to larger multi-agent coordination tasks without adaptation, as measured by task success dropping below 80% when directly applied to 10-agent systems.

BACKGROUND:  
Emergent compositional communication promises systematic generalization in multi-agent systems but has been primarily validated in simple sender-receiver pairs. The assumption that such compositional protocols transfer intact to larger populations performing complex coordination remains untested, leaving open whether template transfer alone suffices for scalable communication.

APPROACH:  
We first train a sender-receiver pair using the publicly available Multi-Agent Particle Environment (MPE) on a standard referential game baseline from Lazaridou et al. (2019) via template transfer training. Then, without further adaptation, we deploy the fixed receiver and newly trained senders in a 10-agent cooperative navigation task within MPE, measuring performance using the standardized average episode success rate defined as the percentage of episodes in which all agents reach their distinct goals without collisions or deadlocks.

EXPERIMENT:  
Success is quantified as the percentage of episodes with full task completion across 1000 evaluation episodes in the 10-agent cooperative navigation task, with an 80% success rate threshold for falsification of scalability. This evaluation protocol and environment are publicly accessible and well-established for multi-agent coordination research.

NOVELTY:  
This work is the first systematic empirical test of the scalability of template transfer-induced compositional protocols beyond dyadic referential settings, explicitly addressing confounds by fixing the receiver and avoiding confounding adaptation effects, and operationalizing task success with rigorous, reproducible metrics on a non-trivial multi-agent coordination benchmark.

topic: Emergent communication in multi-agent systems
text:
IDEA: Autonomous multi-agent systems can learn emergent communication protocols in partially observable environments that achieve at least 90% of the data throughput and latency efficiency of engineered communication models assuming fully optimized channels.

BACKGROUND: Conventional 6G communication theory prioritizes optimizing physical channels and environmental factors to maximize data rate and minimize latency, assuming emergent communication without explicit channel modeling underperforms. However, this overlooks the potential of decentralized, adaptive protocol learning in uncontrolled or noisy real-world settings where channel optimization is infeasible. Demonstrating emergent protocols’ competitive efficiency challenges the prevailing assumption that channel/environment optimization is strictly necessary for high-performance communication.

APPROACH: We train agents in the Multi-Agent Particle Environment (MPE) to develop emergent communication protocols through reinforcement learning, directly measuring effective bits transmitted per timestep and end-to-end message latency by encoding discrete messages into bit representations and normalizing for message length and overhead. We compare performance quantitatively to the CommNet baseline (Sukhbaatar et al., 2016) on cooperative navigation tasks, isolating communication efficiency by controlling for non-communication coordination through ablation studies and communication channel perturbations.

EXPERIMENT: Using publicly available MPE code and pretrained CommNet agents, we measure data rate as bits communicated per episode normalized by duration, and latency as average timestep delay from message emission to effective use. Success is defined by emergent protocols reaching ≥90% of CommNet’s data rate and latency across three independent runs, with ablation confirming communication—not environmental exploitation—is responsible for gains.

NOVELTY: This work operationalizes communication efficiency metrics in a reinforcement-learning multi-agent setting, rigorously disentangling communication quality from task performance, and empirically tests emergent protocols against a well-established CommNet baseline, providing the first quantitative falsification threshold challenging the 6G assumption that channel optimization is a prerequisite for high-performance communication.

topic: Emergent communication in multi-agent systems
text:
IDEA:  
Emergent communication protocols learned via multi-agent reinforcement learning can achieve at least 90% of the spectral efficiency of classical CSI-optimized beamforming in stochastic wireless channels without any explicit channel or environment optimization.

BACKGROUND:  
Current wireless communication design, especially in 6G, assumes that near-optimal performance requires detailed channel state information and environment optimization such as beamforming tailored to the physical channel. This reliance restricts system adaptability in uncontrolled, time-varying environments where perfect CSI is unavailable or costly. Demonstrating that distributed agents can autonomously develop robust communication strategies under such conditions challenges this foundational assumption and could transform communication system design.

APPROACH:  
We simulate a multi-agent communication system using the publicly available DeepMIMO dataset with stochastic channel variations to mimic realistic, time-varying wireless environments. A multi-agent reinforcement learning framework trains agents from scratch with no explicit channel input or environment tuning to develop emergent communication protocols. Performance is benchmarked against a classical perfect-CSI beamforming baseline operating under the same power and bandwidth constraints.

EXPERIMENT:  
We measure averaged spectral efficiency over randomized, unseen channel realizations in DeepMIMO, ensuring identical system constraints for both emergent and baseline systems. A numeric falsification threshold is set at 90% of the baseline’s mean spectral efficiency. Channel state inputs are ablated from the MARL agents to eliminate implicit channel knowledge leakage. Training uses established exploration strategies with convergence diagnostics to confirm stable protocol emergence.

NOVELTY:  
Unlike prior works that rely on environment-aware optimization or handcrafted communication schemes, this study rigorously tests whether purely emergent, environment-agnostic protocols can approach classical performance benchmarks in realistic stochastic wireless channels. It explicitly controls for implicit channel knowledge, standardizes metrics, and sets a clear numeric threshold, addressing key experimental critiques and providing a definitive evaluation of emergent communication adaptability.

topic: Emergent communication in multi-agent systems
text:
IDEA:  
Emergent communication protocols in heterogeneous human-AI multi-agent networks with conflicting goals and constrained autonomy degrade coordination effectiveness compared to fully autonomous, reliably communicating AI baselines, due to fundamentally altered communication semantics and protocol structures.

BACKGROUND:  
Most multi-agent systems research assumes full agent autonomy and reliable communication, enabling emergent protocols that sustain or improve cooperation. However, in realistic human-AI networks where agents have bounded rationality, limited autonomy, and conflicting objectives, these assumptions break down, leaving open whether emergent communication can still yield effective coordination or instead deteriorates. Understanding this gap is critical for designing robust coordination in real-world heterogeneous systems.

APPROACH:  
We model human agents as bounded-rational policies learned via constrained reinforcement learning with limited action sets, paired with AI agents using CommNet architectures in the Multi-Particle Environment (MPE). We introduce conflicting reward structures and autonomy constraints while measuring emergent communication through explicit metrics—message entropy, mutual information between communicated messages and actions, and coordination indices—to isolate communication quality from agent competence. Control conditions vary autonomy and communication independently to disentangle their effects.

EXPERIMENT:  
Run MPE tasks with mixed human-modeled and AI agents under conflicting goals and limited autonomy, comparing episode rewards and communication metrics to a CommNet baseline with full autonomy and reliable communication; establish a falsification threshold at 0.9× baseline reward and statistically test for significant degradation in both reward and communication quality.

NOVELTY:  
Unlike prior work assuming ideal autonomy and communication, this study explicitly isolates the impact of autonomy constraints and goal conflicts on emergent communication quality using rigorous communication-specific metrics and controls; it focuses on realistic human-AI heterogeneity rather than homogeneous AI agent populations, directly addressing gaps in coordination theory for mixed-agent systems.

topic: Emergent communication in multi-agent systems
text:
IDEA:  
Emergent communication protocols developed by multi-agent reinforcement learning within environment-aware 6G mmWave networks can improve average user data rate and end-to-end latency by at least 10% over an environment-aware classical beamforming and adaptive modulation baseline.

BACKGROUND:  
Traditional 6G wireless research primarily optimizes transmitter-receiver design assuming fixed, environment-agnostic protocols, limiting adaptability to dynamic, multi-node network contexts. While environment-level optimizations exist, the potential of autonomous multi-agent systems to develop emergent, coordinated communication strategies that exploit environmental states remains underexplored and unquantified with rigorous statistical validation. This gap hinders progress toward adaptive, cooperative 6G systems needed for massive connectivity and low latency.

APPROACH:  
We train a multi-agent system via centralized training with decentralized execution using reinforcement learning, where each agent controls a node (base station or user equipment) in the DeepMIMO 6G mmWave dataset environment. Agents learn to coordinate beamforming and resource allocation through emergent communication channels, with full environment state information shared equally between baseline and agents to control for environment awareness. Performance is compared to an environment-aware classical baseline employing zero-forcing beamforming and adaptive modulation with identical channel state inputs.

EXPERIMENT:  
Using the publicly available DeepMIMO dataset, we measure the average per-user data rate and 95th percentile latency over 50 independent simulation runs with different random seeds to ensure statistical rigor. Success is defined as achieving ≥10% improvement in mean data rate or latency reduction over the baseline with p<0.05 (t-test) confidence.

NOVELTY:  
This work uniquely isolates the effect of emergent multi-agent communication by controlling for environment awareness in both baseline and agents, providing statistically rigorous evaluation of end-to-end gains in realistic 6G mmWave environments. Unlike prior static or single-agent approaches, it demonstrates multi-agent protocol emergence that leverages environment context beyond classical beamforming adaptations.

topic: Quantum advantage in machine learning tasks
text:
IDEA:  
Evaluate whether quantum-inspired or hybrid classical-quantum models achieve at least a 5% absolute accuracy improvement over classical ResNet-18 on Fashion-MNIST under rigorously matched computational budgets and hyperparameter optimization, thereby demonstrating a quantum advantage on real-world noisy data.

BACKGROUND:  
While classical deep learning is widely presumed sufficient for many practical machine learning tasks, this assumption has not been rigorously tested against quantum-inspired or hybrid models under realistic noise and complexity conditions. Existing work largely demonstrates that classical models can learn classically hard problems efficiently from data, but often lacks strict resource parity and controls for hyperparameter tuning, leaving open whether quantum methods can surpass classical baselines in practical, noisy scenarios.

APPROACH:  
Train a classical ResNet-18 and a quantum-inspired/hybrid model using identical computational budgets defined by total floating-point operations (FLOPs) and wall-clock time measured on the same hardware. Both models undergo balanced, automated hyperparameter searches (e.g., Bayesian optimization) constrained to equal tuning effort and matched effective model capacity (parameter count within ±10%). Evaluate robustness by analyzing performance variance across multiple random seeds and noise augmentations applied consistently to both datasets.

EXPERIMENT:  
Train and evaluate both models on the Fashion-MNIST dataset, using classification accuracy as the primary metric. The falsification threshold is a minimum 5% absolute accuracy increase by the quantum or hybrid model over the classical ResNet-18 baseline, measured on a held-out test set and verified with a minimum of 5 independent runs for statistical significance (p<0.05).

NOVELTY:  
This study provides the first rigorously controlled, resource-matched empirical comparison of classical and quantum-inspired/hybrid models on a real-world noisy benchmark with explicit, quantifiable computational budget constraints and balanced hyperparameter optimization—addressing critical confounds in previous quantum advantage claims and enabling reproducible validation of quantum machine learning benefits.

topic: Quantum advantage in machine learning tasks
text:
IDEA:  
Hybrid quantum-classical models trained and evaluated solely via ideal TensorFlow Quantum simulations will exhibit a statistically significant (>15%) accuracy degradation when deployed on calibrated noisy superconducting quantum hardware without hardware-specific retraining, demonstrating that TFQ simulations do not reliably predict real-device performance.

BACKGROUND:  
Current quantum machine learning research relies heavily on TFQ simulations assuming near-ideal quantum circuits to prototype hybrid models, implicitly trusting their predictive power for hardware deployment. However, noise, gate errors, and hardware constraints in real devices may cause a substantial performance gap that simulation environments neglect, undermining the validity of simulation-based benchmarks and algorithm design decisions.

APPROACH:  
We will train the benchmark hybrid quantum-classical model from Havlíček et al. (2019) on the MNIST dataset using TFQ’s ideal simulator, then deploy the trained model parameters "as is" on a well-characterized superconducting quantum processor with up-to-date calibration and optimized qubit mapping to minimize hardware-specific confounds. By fixing shot counts sufficiently high (e.g., ≥10,000 per measurement) and repeating measurements across multiple calibration cycles, we isolate the fidelity gap attributable to noise and simulate-to-hardware mismatch rather than statistical error or hardware drift.

EXPERIMENT:  
Train the baseline model on MNIST with TFQ ideal simulation, then evaluate its classification accuracy on the same test set using real noisy hardware under controlled conditions; compute the absolute accuracy drop and test whether it exceeds 15%, the falsification threshold.

NOVELTY:  
This study explicitly isolates and quantifies the real-world accuracy degradation of TFQ-trained hybrid quantum-classical models without hardware-specific retraining or noise-aware calibration, addressing confounding factors highlighted by experimentalists and establishing a rigorous numeric threshold for simulation-to-hardware fidelity, which prior work has not systematically benchmarked.

topic: Quantum advantage in machine learning tasks
text:
IDEA:  
Classical theoretical prediction error bounds fail to tightly characterize finite-data regime performance on real-world datasets, enabling quantum-inspired kernel methods to outperform classical RBF-kernel SVMs by more than 5% relative test error on standard benchmarks.

BACKGROUND:  
While classical learning theory provides asymptotic error guarantees for models like SVMs with RBF kernels, it remains unclear whether these bounds hold under practical finite-sample conditions typical of real datasets. The prevailing assumption in both classical and quantum ML communities is that classical models serve as robust baselines with tight error bounds, limiting demonstrated quantum advantages to synthetic or contrived settings. This work targets the gap between theory and practice by empirically challenging these classical guarantees and assessing if quantum-inspired kernels can exploit richer features to surpass classical performance.

APPROACH:  
We conduct a controlled empirical comparison between a classical RBF-kernel SVM and a well-established quantum-inspired kernel method using rigorous, identical hyperparameter tuning protocols and validation schemes to ensure fairness. Performance is measured by classification accuracy on the UCI Wine Quality dataset using fixed, public train/test splits, with a pre-registered falsification threshold defined as a >5% relative decrease in test error of the classical model compared to the quantum-inspired model, computed as:  
\[
\text{Relative Test Error Difference} = \frac{E_{\text{classical}} - E_{\text{quantum}}}{E_{\text{quantum}}}
\]  
where \(E\) is the test error rate (1 - accuracy). If the classical model’s error exceeds this threshold consistently, the hypothesis is confirmed.

EXPERIMENT:  
Train and evaluate classical RBF SVM and quantum-inspired kernel classifiers on the publicly available UCI Wine Quality dataset, using a fixed 70/30 train/test split. Hyperparameters (C, gamma for RBF; feature map parameters for quantum kernel) are optimized via nested cross-validation with identical search budgets. Test error rates are compared via the defined relative error difference metric, with statistical significance assessed over multiple random seeds.

NOVELTY:  
This study is the first to empirically falsify classical asymptotic error bounds in a realistic finite-data regime by demonstrating a statistically significant quantum-inspired kernel advantage on a standard real-world dataset under rigorously controlled conditions. Unlike prior work focusing on synthetic datasets or theoretical asymptotics, it provides actionable evidence challenging the baseline assumptions dominating classical and quantum ML research.

topic: Quantum advantage in machine learning tasks
text:
IDEA:  
Classical machine learning models, including rigorously tuned Random Forests and deep neural networks, exhibit significantly reduced predictive accuracy below 85% on the noisy, real-world UCI HAR dataset’s most challenging activity classification tasks, thereby empirically restoring a practical quantum advantage over prior classical baselines.

BACKGROUND:  
Existing claims of quantum advantage in machine learning often rely on synthetic or idealized datasets where classical methods appear fundamentally limited. Recent work ([P1]) has challenged this by showing classical models can achieve strong performance on supposedly classically hard tasks, but these results overlook the impact of real-world noise and data complexity. It remains unresolved whether classical models maintain their performance advantage when confronted with authentic, noisy datasets representative of practical conditions.

APPROACH:  
We train a Random Forest classifier with extensive hyperparameter tuning via nested cross-validation to ensure optimal classical baseline performance on the UCI HAR dataset’s recognized difficult subtasks. We then compare these results to reported quantum-enhanced methods evaluated under consistent data splits and preprocessing, setting an explicit 85% accuracy threshold as the falsification criterion. This minimal experiment is immediately runnable, reproducible, and controls for noise and preprocessing confounds by strictly adhering to the original dataset conditions.

EXPERIMENT:  
Train and validate Random Forest classifiers on the UCI HAR dataset using 10-fold stratified cross-validation with grid search for hyperparameters (e.g., number of trees, max depth). Measure accuracy on held-out test folds for the hardest activity classes as defined in prior quantum benchmark literature; failure to exceed 85% accuracy confirms the hypothesis.

NOVELTY:  
This study rigorously closes gaps in prior comparisons by enforcing strict classical baseline optimization and consistent experimental conditions, explicitly quantifying the effect of real-world noise on classical learning limits. Unlike previous synthetic or lightly preprocessed benchmarks, it provides the first empirical evidence that noise and data complexity can restore a meaningful quantum advantage in practical machine learning tasks.

topic: Quantum advantage in machine learning tasks
text:
IDEA: Demonstrate a statistically significant quantum advantage exceeding 2% in robust classification accuracy and complementary metrics on noisy Fashion-MNIST data, directly comparing variational quantum classifiers to a rigorously optimized classical ResNet-18 baseline under equal computational budgets.

BACKGROUND: The potential of quantum machine learning (QML) to outperform classical models on noisy, real-world datasets remains unresolved, especially given claims that classical deep learning can efficiently solve classically hard problems under realistic noise conditions. Prior demonstrations often rely on idealized noise models or single metrics, leaving open whether near-term quantum models can deliver a practical advantage in realistic data regimes.

APPROACH: We train a variational quantum classifier using quantum kernel methods on Fashion-MNIST augmented with realistic, class-dependent noise and compare it to a classical ResNet-18 baseline whose hyperparameters and architectures are exhaustively optimized via automated search within identical GPU-time constraints. Evaluation employs multiple metrics—accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, calibration error, and robustness to noise perturbations—to avoid ambiguity from single-metric reliance.

EXPERIMENT: Both models will be trained on the publicly available Fashion-MNIST dataset with synthetic noise calibrated to reflect empirical noise distributions from image acquisition. Performance is assessed on a held-out noisy test set, and a quantum advantage is claimed if the quantum model outperforms the classical baseline by at least 2% in classification accuracy while showing consistent improvements in secondary metrics, with statistical significance verified via repeated cross-validation.

NOVELTY: Unlike prior work focusing on idealized conditions or single evaluation metrics, this study rigorously controls for hyperparameter optimization fairness and employs a comprehensive metric suite to validate quantum advantage claims on noisy, real-world data. The experimental design explicitly balances compute resources and noise realism, addressing known confounds and providing the first reproducible empirical benchmark for quantum advantage in practical learning tasks.

topic: Topological methods for high-dimensional data analysis
text:
IDEA:  
Mapper-based topological representations of scRNA-seq data exhibit significantly lower robustness than t-SNE embeddings in preserving continuous cell differentiation trajectories under realistic noise and batch effect perturbations.

BACKGROUND:  
While Mapper and other Topological Data Analysis methods are believed to robustly capture global data shape in high-dimensional biological data, their stability under realistic experimental variability remains unquantified. Current evaluations often rely on cluster-based metrics that fail to measure preservation of continuous biological trajectories, leaving an open problem in assessing topological versus nonlinear embedding robustness in single-cell RNA-seq analyses.

APPROACH:  
We will directly compare Mapper and t-SNE on publicly available scRNA-seq datasets by quantifying trajectory preservation using pseudotime correlation and graph edit distance metrics alongside silhouette scores computed on annotated differentiation trajectories. Parameter optimization for Mapper and t-SNE will be systematically performed with cross-validation to ensure balanced tuning. Noise and batch effects will be simulated using established single-cell batch simulation frameworks (e.g., Splatter) to generate biologically realistic perturbations.

EXPERIMENT:  
Using the PBMC 3k dataset from 10x Genomics, we will generate perturbed versions with Splatter-modeled batch effects and technical noise, then produce low-dimensional embeddings via optimized Mapper and t-SNE pipelines. Preservation of cell differentiation trajectories will be quantified by changes in pseudotime correlation and graph edit distance relative to unperturbed data; a >10% greater degradation in Mapper’s metrics compared to t-SNE will confirm the hypothesis.

NOVELTY:  
This study rigorously challenges the assumption of Mapper’s inherent robustness by combining trajectory-specific metrics with realistic batch effect simulations and balanced parameter tuning, providing the first quantitative benchmark of topological versus nonlinear embedding stability in preserving continuous biological processes in scRNA-seq data.

topic: Topological methods for high-dimensional data analysis
text:
IDEA:  
Quantitatively benchmark the biological interpretability of Mapper against PHATE and TriMap on publicly available single-cell RNA-seq datasets using comprehensive clustering and trajectory metrics, testing whether Mapper’s topological insights yield a ≥10% improvement.

BACKGROUND:  
Mapper is widely claimed to surpass conventional nonlinear dimensionality reduction methods like t-SNE by capturing continuous trajectories and branching structures in scRNA-seq data, yet its practical biological interpretability advantage over newer nonlinear methods such as PHATE and TriMap remains unproven. Current evaluations often rely on simplistic clustering metrics that fail to capture trajectory and topological features, leaving Mapper’s true value in high-dimensional biological data analysis an open question.

APPROACH:  
We will apply Mapper, PHATE, and TriMap to multiple publicly available single-cell RNA-seq datasets—including PBMC 3k and at least two additional diverse datasets—with Mapper’s parameters exhaustively optimized via grid search guided by domain expertise to ensure parity with well-tuned PHATE and TriMap settings. Biological interpretability will be quantified using both clustering metrics (Adjusted Rand Index, silhouette score) and trajectory/topology-aware metrics (pseudotime correlation with known differentiation timelines, branch purity, and graph connectivity measures) to capture continuous and branching structures.

EXPERIMENT:  
Run all methods under comparable computational budgets on standard hardware; evaluate biological interpretability by measuring ARI, silhouette, and pseudotime correlation against expert-annotated cell types and known differentiation trajectories. The falsification threshold is Mapper failing to improve PHATE’s performance by at least 10% on a composite interpretability score aggregated from these metrics.

NOVELTY:  
This study uniquely integrates trajectory- and topology-specific quantitative metrics alongside clustering evaluations, applies rigorous parameter optimization across multiple datasets, and sets a clear numeric falsification criterion—addressing previous oversights that conflated Mapper’s theoretical appeal with insufficient empirical validation and providing the first statistically robust, reproducible benchmark of topological versus nonlinear dimensionality reduction methods in single-cell biology.

topic: Topological methods for high-dimensional data analysis
text:
IDEA:  
Mapper’s topological summaries do not reliably preserve biologically meaningful pseudotemporal trajectories in scRNA-seq data, whereas diffusion-based methods like PHATE and diffusion maps quantitatively outperform Mapper in trajectory fidelity when benchmarked using standardized, reproducible pseudotime extraction protocols.

BACKGROUND:  
Although Mapper is widely used in single-cell analysis to infer and visualize cellular trajectories via topological summaries, it lacks a standardized method for extracting linear pseudotime, and its trajectory preservation has not been rigorously benchmarked against recent nonlinear manifold learning methods. Current assumptions that Mapper’s outputs inherently reflect meaningful biological progressions remain untested quantitatively, limiting confidence in its biological interpretability.

APPROACH:  
We develop a rigorously defined, reproducible procedure to infer pseudotime from Mapper graphs by (1) selecting root nodes based on known early progenitor cell clusters, (2) computing shortest-path distances within the Mapper graph to all other nodes, and (3) mapping these distances back to cells for scalar pseudotime assignment. We benchmark this against PHATE and diffusion maps pseudotime inferred directly from their embeddings, ensuring optimal parameter tuning via grid search and cross-validation for all methods to avoid confounding by suboptimal settings.

EXPERIMENT:  
Using the publicly available Paul et al. hematopoiesis scRNA-seq dataset with established biological cell ordering, we compute Kendall’s tau correlations between method-inferred pseudotime and ground-truth progression. A falsification threshold requires Mapper’s score to be below 0.7 while PHATE and diffusion maps score ≥0.8 to confirm its inferior trajectory preservation. All analyses include batch correction and standardized preprocessing to control noise and confounds.

NOVELTY:  
This study is the first to rigorously define and standardize pseudotime extraction from Mapper outputs for fair quantitative comparison with diffusion-based methods on real biological data, providing critical benchmarking that challenges the untested community assumption of Mapper’s biological trajectory fidelity.

topic: Topological methods for high-dimensional data analysis
text:
IDEA:  
Quantitatively compare the biological interpretability of Mapper-generated topological networks versus UMAP embeddings in single-cell RNA-seq data by rigorously mapping both outputs to cluster-level expression profiles and evaluating lineage-specific marker gene correlations, testing whether Mapper improves correlation by ≥0.05 over UMAP.

BACKGROUND:  
Topological Data Analysis methods like Mapper are theorized to better capture complex, continuous differentiation trajectories in high-dimensional single-cell RNA-seq data than ubiquitous nonlinear embeddings like UMAP. However, the lack of standardized, quantitative evaluations comparing Mapper’s biological interpretability to UMAP, especially accounting for their fundamentally different output formats, leaves its practical advantage unproven. This gap challenges informed choices of visualization tools for biological insight extraction from scRNA-seq.

APPROACH:  
We propose converting Mapper’s network nodes to cluster-averaged gene expression vectors and summarizing UMAP embeddings by per-cell coordinates; then, for each lineage-specific marker gene, compute Pearson correlations of marker expression with corresponding cluster averages (Mapper) or cell embeddings (UMAP). Parameter spaces for Mapper (filter functions, clustering resolution) and UMAP (neighbors, min-dist) will be systematically optimized via grid search to fairly maximize marker correlation. The key hypothesis is that Mapper will improve marker correlation by at least +0.05 compared to UMAP.

EXPERIMENT:  
Using the publicly available Paul et al. mouse bone marrow scRNA-seq dataset and a curated set of lineage-specific marker genes, generate Mapper graphs and UMAP embeddings with optimized parameters. Compute Pearson correlation coefficients between marker expression and embedding features aggregated at cluster (Mapper) or cell (UMAP) level, and test whether Mapper’s correlations exceed UMAP’s by ≥0.05. All code and parameter selection criteria will be fully documented for reproducibility.

NOVELTY:  
This study establishes a principled, standardized framework to quantitatively compare Mapper’s discrete topological outputs with continuous manifold embeddings on biological interpretability metrics, explicitly addressing the critical challenge of non-comparable output formats and hyperparameter biases—an aspect missing from prior qualitative or heuristic comparisons in scRNA-seq visualization literature.

topic: Topological methods for high-dimensional data analysis
text:
IDEA: Quantitatively benchmark and demonstrate that nonlinear dimensionality reduction methods (PHATE and diffusion maps) outperform Mapper in preserving continuous biological trajectories from scRNA-seq data using rigorously validated pseudotime and topology metrics.

BACKGROUND: While Mapper is widely regarded as a topological baseline for capturing complex high-dimensional cellular differentiation trajectories, its performance relative to modern nonlinear dimensionality reduction (NLDR) methods remains unclear due to ambiguous evaluation metrics and inconsistent parameter tuning. Existing comparisons often rely on discrete or partial stage annotations and qualitative visualization, failing to rigorously validate trajectory preservation or address sensitivity to preprocessing and parameter settings.

APPROACH: We perform a standardized, reproducible comparison of Mapper, PHATE, and diffusion maps on the Paul et al. (2015) hematopoiesis scRNA-seq dataset, applying exhaustive, method-specific parameter optimization and uniform preprocessing to eliminate bias. We evaluate trajectory preservation using multiple complementary, well-validated metrics—including Kendall’s tau correlation against a continuous pseudotime derived from Slingshot (a lineage-aware method), branch assignment accuracy, and topological similarity scores—to robustly quantify performance differences.

EXPERIMENT: Using publicly available Paul et al. (2015) data, we compute pseudotime trajectories with each method, optimize parameters via grid search, and assess performance by 1) Kendall’s tau correlation to continuous Slingshot pseudotime with a 10% improvement threshold over Mapper as a numeric falsification criterion, and 2) branch assignment F1 scores and Mapper’s topological network consistency, ensuring reproducibility through fixed random seeds and public code.

NOVELTY: This work uniquely combines rigorous, continuous pseudotime ground truth and multiple quantitative metrics with comprehensive, balanced parameter tuning across methods, directly addressing prior ambiguities and reproducibility issues to definitively test the assumption that Mapper’s explicit topological representation best preserves biological trajectories in scRNA-seq data.

topic: Mechanistic interpretability of transformer models
text:
IDEA:  
Empirically test whether structured, taxonomy-based surveys improve newcomer understanding and research efficiency in mechanistic interpretability of transformers by comparing them against unstructured literature exploration using standardized, objectively scored assessments.

BACKGROUND:  
Mechanistic interpretability (MI) of transformer models is a rapidly evolving field with numerous expert-curated surveys claiming to facilitate newcomer learning and accelerate research. However, these claims remain anecdotal and unvalidated by rigorous experimentation. Without empirical evidence, it is unclear if structured survey taxonomies meaningfully reduce cognitive load or improve research productivity compared to traditional, unstructured literature search.

APPROACH:  
Recruit participants with minimal prior MI exposure and randomly assign them to study MI literature either via a recent, publicly available taxonomy-based survey (e.g., the 2024 Practical Review) or through keyword-guided, unstructured exploration of the same corpus (Papers with Code MI papers + Semantic Scholar filtered set). Evaluate understanding through a validated multiple-choice test covering core MI concepts and methods, and measure research efficiency by timed, standardized interpretability problem-solving tasks with pre-registered scoring rubrics and inter-rater reliability to ensure objectivity.

EXPERIMENT:  
Use a sufficiently powered sample (N≥60) to detect at least a 20% relative improvement in mean test scores or task completion quality/time between groups, with pre-registered analysis plans controlling for participant prior knowledge and learning preferences via stratified randomization and covariate adjustment.

NOVELTY:  
Unlike prior expert-curated surveys or descriptive reviews, this study rigorously operationalizes and quantitatively tests the impact of survey structure on learning outcomes and research productivity in MI using objective, reproducible metrics and controlled experimental design, filling a critical gap in interpretability research methodology and science communication.

topic: Mechanistic interpretability of transformer models
text:
IDEA:  
Empirically evaluate whether a taxonomy-guided approach to mechanistic interpretability of transformer models improves researcher efficiency and accuracy of component function identification by at least 20% compared to standard literature review methods on GPT-2 small using a rigorously defined benchmark.

BACKGROUND:  
Mechanistic interpretability (MI) of transformers aims to reverse-engineer model components like neurons and attention heads, but prevailing assumptions claim that taxonomy-based frameworks substantially improve research outcomes and efficiency without direct empirical validation. Existing MI surveys and taxonomies are rich but remain untested against traditional, heuristic literature review methods, leaving open whether these frameworks truly aid interpretability or if the field’s methods are immature and fragmented.

APPROACH:  
We define an operational metric for interpretability accuracy by establishing a standardized ground truth dataset of known neuron and head functions from prior published ablations and activation patching results on GPT-2 small with WikiText-2. We then conduct a controlled, randomized user study assigning equally expert researchers to either taxonomy-guided or baseline literature review methods, measuring time-to-conclusion and agreement with ground truth annotations to quantify accuracy. Strict protocols and blinding ensure researcher bias is minimized and expertise balanced across methods.

EXPERIMENT:  
Apply both taxonomy-guided and baseline literature review approaches to analyze GPT-2 small’s internal activations on WikiText-2, measuring (1) percentage agreement with established ground truth component functions for interpretability accuracy, and (2) researcher time-to-conclusion. A ≥20% improvement in either metric (p < 0.05, two-tailed test) will falsify the hypothesis that taxonomies do not provide meaningful benefits.

NOVELTY:  
This is the first rigorous empirical comparison of taxonomy-guided mechanistic interpretability against conventional literature review grounded in objective, reproducible accuracy metrics and controlled researcher assignment, addressing a critical methodological assumption in MI research that has, until now, been purely speculative.

topic: Mechanistic interpretability of transformer models
text:
IDEA: Evaluate whether a task-centric taxonomy improves novice researchers’ ability to identify effective mechanistic interpretability methods for transformers compared to unstructured literature review, using a predefined quantitative benchmark and a 20% improvement threshold.

BACKGROUND: Mechanistic interpretability (MI) of transformer models relies on selecting appropriate analysis methods, yet it is unclear if taxonomies that organize methods by task truly aid researchers in discovering impactful techniques. Existing surveys assume these taxonomies enhance research efficiency, but no empirical evidence tests their predictive utility or practical advantage for guiding new MI investigations. Clarifying this will inform the value of structured knowledge frameworks in MI.

APPROACH: Recruit skill-matched novice researchers and randomly assign them to two groups: one provided with the established task-centric taxonomy of interpretability methods, the other given an unstructured, comprehensive literature review. Both groups apply chosen methods to a fixed benchmark task (e.g., syntactic probing on GPT-2 Small) within equal time and compute budgets. Method effectiveness is evaluated by predefined, objective performance metrics on benchmark tasks, with “promising methods” defined as those achieving statistically significant improvements meeting or exceeding fixed thresholds.

EXPERIMENT: Use publicly available datasets for syntactic probing on GPT-2 Small as the benchmark; measure success by the number of methods each group identifies that improve probing accuracy by at least 5 percentage points over baseline with p < 0.05 (Bonferroni-corrected). Statistical power analysis will determine sample size to detect a minimum 20% relative increase in effective method discovery; time-on-task and motivation will be controlled via standardized protocols and surveys.

NOVELTY: This is the first controlled, quantitative evaluation of a mechanistic interpretability taxonomy’s utility as a research guide, rigorously operationalizing interpretability method success and controlling confounds that prior descriptive or process-oriented works overlook. It challenges untested assumptions about curated taxonomies and produces actionable insights into structuring MI research tools.

topic: Mechanistic interpretability of transformer models
text:
IDEA:  
Evaluate whether transformer-based LLMs fine-tuned on materials science tasks produce experimentally invalid mechanistic explanations at rates exceeding 30%, challenging the assumption that their mechanistic outputs reliably reflect true physical relationships.

BACKGROUND:  
Mechanistic interpretability aims to understand if LLMs capture real-world causal or physical relationships, yet this remains untested in complex scientific domains like materials science. While fine-tuned LLMs show promise in generating explanations, the fidelity of these mechanistic outputs against experimental truth has not been rigorously quantified, leaving a critical gap in trusting LLM-generated scientific hypotheses.

APPROACH:  
Fine-tune an accessible transformer LLM (e.g., OpenAI’s GPT or an open checkpoint like LLaMA) on the MatBench suite with explicit mechanistic labels, then prompt the model with standardized, structured queries to generate mechanistic explanations for test samples. Evaluate outputs using a pre-defined rubric combining cross-validation against curated databases (e.g., Materials Project, ICSD) and blinded expert assessment with consensus criteria specifying “experimentally invalid” as contradictions to established physical laws or reproducible experimental results.

EXPERIMENT:  
Run the fine-tuned model on held-out MatBench tasks, collect mechanistic explanations under fixed prompt templates to minimize prompt-induced variance, and measure the fraction of invalid outputs with a numeric falsification threshold set at 30%. Use dual independent expert reviews plus database cross-referencing to ensure reproducibility and consistency.

NOVELTY:  
This study is the first to quantitatively benchmark mechanistic interpretability of LLMs in materials science with a transparent, reproducible validity criterion and a rigorously controlled prompting methodology, directly addressing expert critiques of subjectivity and confounding factors in explanation evaluation. It uniquely tests mechanistic output fidelity beyond correlation-based performance, providing actionable insights into the scientific reliability of transformer-generated mechanistic hypotheses.

topic: Mechanistic interpretability of transformer models
text:
IDEA:  
Evaluate whether a task-centric taxonomy improves newcomers’ mechanistic interpretability accuracy on a standardized transformer circuit identification benchmark by more than 5% compared to a taxonomy-free literature review.

BACKGROUND:  
Mechanistic interpretability (MI) of transformers is complex, and newcomers struggle to learn how to identify internal circuits and interpret model behaviors. While a task-centric taxonomy has been proposed to structure MI knowledge and reduce cognitive load, it remains unclear if this pedagogical approach measurably enhances newcomers’ practical interpretability performance versus conventional, unstructured study. Defining clear, objective measures and controlling study conditions is crucial to rigorously evaluating the taxonomy’s real-world utility.

APPROACH:  
Recruit two matched cohorts of ML novices; one studies a carefully curated task-centric taxonomy of MI techniques, while the other studies an equivalent set of seminal MI papers without taxonomy guidance. Both groups undergo the same controlled study schedule with tracked engagement time to neutralize confounds. Their knowledge is then assessed using a pre-validated benchmark dataset (e.g., Open Interpretability Mechanistic Benchmark, OIMB) with expert-annotated ground-truth circuits and behaviors, scored via a standardized rubric adjudicated by multiple experts to produce an objective accuracy metric.

EXPERIMENT:  
Run a one-week study on a single GPU where cohorts complete the same predefined interpretability tasks on the OIMB dataset. Measure accuracy as the percentage of correctly identified circuits and valid behavioral interpretations per expert consensus. The hypothesis is falsified if the taxonomy group outperforms the baseline by more than 5% accuracy, demonstrating meaningful pedagogical benefit.

NOVELTY:  
This is the first empirical evaluation of a task-centric MI taxonomy’s impact on newcomer interpretability performance using a rigorously defined, expert-validated quantitative benchmark and controlled study design that accounts for engagement and effort confounds. Prior work has focused on taxonomic survey or automated circuit discovery without assessing how knowledge organization affects learner outcomes.

topic: Zero-shot generalization in reinforcement learning
text:
IDEA: Limited exteroceptive sensory inputs combined with proprioception significantly improve zero-shot locomotion generalization on novel terrains compared to proprioception-only controllers.

BACKGROUND: Zero-shot generalization in reinforcement learning for legged locomotion remains challenging, especially on unseen, structurally diverse terrains. Prevailing methods typically rely solely on proprioceptive feedback, assuming it suffices for robust control. This assumption neglects whether minimal exteroceptive sensing can fundamentally enhance generalization beyond proprioceptive baselines.

APPROACH: We train two DeepMind Control Suite TerrainRLSim policies with identical architectures and hyperparameters—one using proprioceptive inputs only, the other augmented with low-dimensional exteroceptive terrain heightmaps. Both policies are trained on a fixed set of procedurally generated terrains and evaluated zero-shot on rigorously held-out novel terrain distributions under matched episode lengths and termination criteria, measuring average episode return and statistical significance.

EXPERIMENT: Using the publicly available DeepMind Control Suite with TerrainRLSim, we run 30 evaluation episodes per held-out terrain type, defining termination by fall or fixed horizon (1000 steps). We compare mean returns and apply paired statistical tests, falsifying the null if the proprioceptive-only policy achieves ≤50% of the augmented policy’s mean return with p < 0.05.

NOVELTY: Unlike prior work focusing solely on proprioception or rich exteroceptive modalities without strict controls, this study isolates minimal exteroceptive sensing’s causal effect on zero-shot generalization with rigorously matched conditions and statistically grounded thresholds, providing the first quantitative evidence that minimal exteroception is critical for scalable terrain generalization in RL locomotion.

topic: Zero-shot generalization in reinforcement learning
text:
