IDEA: Controllers trained solely on proprioceptive feedback exhibit a quantifiable and reproducible degradation below 50% normalized success rate in zero-shot locomotion tasks on significantly morphologically altered DeepMind Control Suite agents, demonstrating limited generality of proprioceptive-only sensing.

BACKGROUND: While proprioception is fundamental for biological locomotion and supports robust control in fixed robot morphologies, its efficacy for zero-shot transfer across novel robot morphologies or sensor configurations remains unclear. Prior work often assumes proprioceptive feedback generalizes well due to its internal-state nature, but no standardized evaluation rigorously quantifies this limitation or isolates sensory modality effects from morphology overfitting.

APPROACH: We train a standard proprioceptive-feedback-only reinforcement learning agent using the publicly available DeepMind Control Suite “Cheetah” and “Walker” environments as baselines. Zero-shot generalization is evaluated on at least two carefully chosen morphologically distinct variants from existing benchmark modifications (e.g., extended limbs, altered joint ranges) with success defined as normalized cumulative reward exceeding 50% of baseline performance, ensuring consistent, numeric falsifiability. Ablations include control comparisons with multi-modal policies incorporating exteroceptive inputs to isolate proprioceptive feedback limitations.

EXPERIMENT: Using the DeepMind Control Suite public datasets and standard proprioceptive state features, train TD3 or SAC agents to convergence on canonical morphologies; evaluate zero-shot performance on at least two morphology-perturbed variants previously used in published robustness benchmarks (e.g., modified “Walker” with longer legs). Measure normalized cumulative reward per episode as the success metric, with failure defined as below 50% of baseline average reward.

NOVELTY: This study uniquely isolates proprioceptive-only sensing in zero-shot morphological transfer, rigorously quantifies performance degradation with a clear numeric threshold, and uses well-characterized, publicly available benchmarks—addressing ambiguity and confounds in prior work while directly challenging the assumption that proprioception alone suffices for generalization in RL locomotion controllers.

topic: Zero-shot generalization in reinforcement learning
text:
IDEA: Incorporating exteroceptive visual input alongside proprioception significantly improves zero-shot locomotion generalization across novel robot morphologies and terrains compared to proprioception-only control.

BACKGROUND: Current RL-based locomotion controllers predominantly rely on proprioceptive feedback and struggle to generalize zero-shot to new morphologies or unseen environments due to insufficient contextual understanding of terrain. Although proprioception captures internal dynamics, it lacks environmental awareness critical for adapting locomotion to novel external conditions.

APPROACH: We augment a baseline proprioceptive PPO agent with RGB-D visual inputs processed through a compact convolutional encoder fused with proprioceptive features, trained end-to-end with identical network capacity and training budgets to isolate sensory contribution. Success is defined by a standardized metric measuring distance traveled without falling over fixed time windows, normalized per morphology to ensure comparability.

EXPERIMENT: Using the DeepMind Control Suite’s legged locomotion tasks, we compare zero-shot success rates—defined as normalized distance before failure—between proprioception-only and proprioception-plus-vision agents on unseen robot morphologies and terrains, requiring at least a 50% relative improvement in success rate for validation. Controlled ablations hold model size and training duration constant to remove confounding factors.

NOVELTY: This work uniquely quantifies the isolated contribution of exteroceptive vision to zero-shot locomotion generalization with rigorous metric standardization and model capacity controls, addressing prior assumptions that proprioception alone suffices and demonstrating when and how multimodal sensory integration yields substantial, robust improvements.

topic: Zero-shot generalization in reinforcement learning
text:
IDEA: Incorporating exteroceptive sensors such as LiDAR and depth cameras alongside proprioceptive feedback significantly improves zero-shot quadrupedal locomotion success rates on physically distinct, unseen terrains compared to proprioception-only controllers.

BACKGROUND: Zero-shot generalization in reinforcement learning for legged robots remains challenging due to drastic variations in terrain properties that the policy has never encountered. Existing proprioceptive-only controllers, like the RMA baseline, assume internal state feedback suffices for robust reactive control but often fail on novel terrain types such as slippery or deformable surfaces. Demonstrating that multimodal sensing yields significant gains would directly address the limitation of purely proprioceptive policies in real-world deployment.

APPROACH: We augment the RMA quadrupedal locomotion policy with simulated exteroceptive sensor inputs (LiDAR and depth camera point clouds) integrated via sensor fusion layers trained end-to-end with domain randomized environment parameters. The combined policy is trained solely in simulation without terrain-specific tuning and evaluated zero-shot on unseen terrains with distinct friction and deformability profiles.

EXPERIMENT: Using the publicly available RMA quadruped environment and dataset, we compare zero-shot locomotion success rates—defined as traversing a fixed 10-meter path without falls or stumbles—between the proprioceptive-only baseline and the augmented multimodal controller. Success is quantified as completion without failure within a maximum time budget, with a falsification threshold set at achieving at least 60% success rate on two unseen terrain types (ice-like and deformable mud), evaluated over 30 randomized trials per terrain and controller.

NOVELTY: This work is the first to rigorously quantify and demonstrate that explicitly integrating exteroceptive inputs in a zero-shot RL quadruped controller trained with domain randomization yields a statistically significant (>10% absolute) improvement in robustness on drastically novel terrains, challenging the prevailing notion that proprioception alone suffices. It addresses prior gaps by defining clear success metrics, using realistic sensor noise models, and controlling for overfitting via multiple seeds and sensor noise perturbations.

topic: Zero-shot generalization in reinforcement learning
text:
IDEA: Abstract state representations that discard pixel-level details impair zero-shot generalization on texture-sensitive visual RL tasks, as evidenced by sub-75% accuracy on Procgen levels with novel, fine-grained texture variants when using the P5 baseline.

BACKGROUND: Zero-shot generalization in reinforcement learning remains challenging, particularly when agents encounter novel visual features unseen during training. While recent work (e.g., P5) advocates that abstract representations improve generalization by ignoring irrelevant pixel details, this assumption neglects tasks requiring subtle visual discriminations, such as texture-based cues critical in Procgen environments. Determining whether abstraction inherently loses critical information is an open question with implications for representation learning in RL.

APPROACH: We replicate the P5 abstract representation learning method on Procgen tasks with fixed training textures and evaluate zero-shot transfer to rigorously validated novel texture variants that demand fine-grained visual discrimination. We quantify performance using mean episode success rates averaged over multiple random seeds and levels, defining failure as accuracy below 75%, a threshold set by prior Procgen baseline performance and supported with 95% confidence intervals to ensure statistical robustness.

EXPERIMENT: Train P5 on Procgen levels with fixed training textures; test zero-shot on a standardized set of novel textures manually validated to require fine-grained visual discrimination (e.g., texture swaps confirmed by human perceptual study). Evaluate mean accuracy over at least 10 seeds per level, compute confidence intervals, and perform significance testing against the 75% threshold.

NOVELTY: Unlike prior work that assumes pixel-level detail abstraction universally aids generalization, this study explicitly challenges that claim by isolating texture-based visual cues and rigorously quantifying zero-shot performance with statistical rigor on publicly available benchmarks and a named baseline (P5). This clarifies the limits of abstract representation learning and motivates hybrid approaches retaining task-relevant fine-grained features.
